THE SHORTEST DAY.
Thick fogs by day now veil from sight The shining orb of life and light, - Whilst in deep snow the fields are clad

And nature isrnot truly glad. IC° varied landscape can we see, Only the snow-wrapt leafless tree, And nature in the longest night Both hide her beauties from our sight. No singing birds or blooming flowers To cheer us in these gloomy hours, But bitter cold now meets the breath— To many bringing pain and death,. Oh love, oh beauty, health and life Is death triumphant in the strife Have ye no hidden power to live Beyond the gloom his shadows give? Is it in vain we live and light— In vain we struggle for the right? Shall love and hope and friendship be But withered leaves upon the tree? Yea, Nature! on this shortest day I love thee; it will pass away. Believing all thy ways are right, I trust thee throught the darkest night.
S. Kenyon.

div.head: Warrington, Dec. 21st, 1890.
div.p: Warrington, Dec. 21st, 1890.
THE TOWN COUNCILLOR.

BY HUGH BETTE. Once upon a time, one of the councillors I know by sight, from one of the towns I know by name, got into a Liverpool train and sat almost opposite to me. Now we have said something before about the peaceful contentment of the town councillor, so I will simply remark that this T.C. had it bad—l mean strongly developed. You don't expect a town councillor to lower himself by familiarity with strangers, of course; so when he barely glanced me over as if to convince himself that I was human, and then settled down to pleasure, I didn't feel alighted. I hope there is no man who thinks that a town councillor hasn't the right to enjoy himself when be is taking a short vacation. This T.C. proceeded to enjoy himself with that serene indifference characteristic of the great man, and with a grace that be/ongeth not to the plebeian. He gently pushed his hat to the back of his neck, spread out his legs,and pointed his toes upwa:ds and outwards. From a capacious pocket he drew a large pomegranate, and cut it in two with his penknife. i We have a right to look for shrewdness tt a town councillor. It is one of the strong points for which we elect him. . The .shrewdness of this T.C. was re- freshing. He didn't put that penknife back in his pocket for the acid to corrode the steel. No! with ealm deliberation he carefully wiped the blade on the carriage cushion; and it was gratifying to reflect that we have at least one long-headed councillor. By the time the train stopped at the first station the T.C. had placed one-half of the pomegranate on the seat beside him, and, with the joint exertions of his teeth and fingers, he had torn off the rind of the other half, and was busily engaged picking out the luscious sections one by one and conveying them to his mouth ; and although the juice squirted all over his hands, he was evidently too sensible a man to permit the presence of other people to interfere with his mode of enjoyment. A woman who had two boys with her got into the compartment. The woman and one boy, by almost. superhuman efforts, managed to wriggle over the councillor's feet, but the smallest boy had to be picked up from amongst the councillor's legs: yet the councillor himself was tranquil; he didn't seem to mind in the least, but kept his eyes steadfastly fixed on his pomegranate, and pecked away at the sections with the extremest good nature. When the woman and herboys got out at the next station, they glared at the councillor in an awful manner; and the way they trod on his feet made ray corns ache; but he never once raised his eyes from that pomegranate. I fancy his mind- mast have been far away in the Council Chamber labouring through the labyrinths of some giant scheme for the benefit of the toiling multitude. While the councillor was wiping his hands on the cushion in an absent-minded sort of way, I thought it a good opportunity to speak to him. " Going far on this train Mr. Blank ?" I inquired. He didn't seem to be surprised at a stranger ad- dressing him by his name; town councillors never are, they take it for granted that everybody knows them, of course. " Aye ! I'm just goin' as far as Liverpool;' he answered. _
from?

" Is business pretty brisk with you Mr. Blank r I asked. "Um !" he assented. ,Le had got the other half of that everlasting vaiwanate, and resumed the pecking process. He ,evidentl want to talk, and considering the r -gusto witht which be passed the fruit into his mouth, I couldn't ‘•,7Tect him to. I watched him e till the scene became so nsely real that I could -almost taste that pomegranate Pviself, and I began to feel a debasing inclination to lJegli picking my teeth there and then. All Of a sudden the idea seemed to strike hifil that be coni‘l utilise me, for he looked up and ' abruptly demanded— " D'yo know owt about parrots Mister ?" "Parrots?" I ejaculated, wondering whatever could have brought a councillor's great mind down to such things. "Parrots, yes !" I said," Ido know a little about parrots." "Well," said the councillor, "I'm goin' to Liver- pool to buy a parrot, an' I thowt you might be able to tell me where I can get a good un, one as can talk." Now it would be going into vain speculations to wonder why a town councillor should want a parrot that could talk. We should imagine that, in the Council Chamber, where there is—but perhaps it isn't wise to chronicle such flitting ideas, so let that pass. I gave Mr. Blank the name of a deafer, and added that it would be best for him to purchase a parrot i that was thoroughly acclimatised, as it would not be so likely to die as one fresh imported. I thought there was a slight look of bewilderment in his face .I,S he returned to the attack on his pomegranate; but I put it down to the recurrence of some knotty problem of the Council Chamber, which might have just flashed across him. When he had inished the very last section, and reluctantly thrown the rind out of the window - (this extra trouble being taken presumably so that the sight of the empty rind might not tantalize him), he almost petrified me with the following question— "'What breed Of a bird did yo' say I was to ask for, Mister?" "Eh! What ?" I exclaimed. thing about breed." "Yhy, yo' did. Cli—clime—climie.k summat." "Oh! acclimatised." "Aye! that's it. Are they them sort wi' red tt, , " Malik," I said, "you know what the word acclimatise means, don't you?" "No!" he replied candidly. "Do you know what a climate is ? " I asked. "Aye," he replied, "a climate's a—aweather like place, a country." "Very well," I said, "when an animal is brougbt Srom a warm climate to a cold one, or vies versa, and it has become inured, or got used to the different temperature to that in which it has lived, we say it is acclimatised. But, of course, you are chaffing me, Mr. Blank; you understand all this." The worthy councillor here indulged in a very griowing laugh, and I continued, "But, putting jokes aside, we can easily understand that when a parrot is brought very quickly from the Arctic regions to England, the chance are ten to one that ltiill die, Eh ?" "Oh yes ?" he understood. Now that we are talking seriously, he entered apon the subject gravely. "To guard against them being starved, however," I resume, " they bring parrots over in refri4eratorB, and cauterize their larynx to prevent resuscita- tion; and this is the sort of parrot I advise you to buy." "Yo' might write that name on a bit of paper:, he said as the train came into Liverpool ; and after I had done so, we were on such good terms that he actually condescended to shake hands at
"I never said any-

parting. Reflecting upon the honour done to me upon this I occasion, I -haven't perhaps such cause to feel sad ' 30 I thought. No! I won't be sad. In fact, I absolutely refuse to be sad. Ha! Ha! H Stay, I was forgetting that this is a serious subject. I had intended to finish with a stage laugh, but it wouldn't be right. Let us finish with becoming dignity. Let us at least reserve the laugh till we have been to Councillor Blank's house, and seen whether he has brought a parrot, and whether it is an acclimatised parrot, or one with a red tail.
A CHRISTMAS BOX, By MARY KYLE DALLAS,
'ES.

"Only five hundred dollars! To think that only five hundred dollars would save the house, and for want of it it must be sold I and what we shall do after that Ido not know " And the handsome young matron who spoke burst into a flood of bitter tears. "It is a shame to worry you with my troubles," she added, in a-moment more; "but really I am in such a state that I can't keep it to myself, Miss Morgan. Mr. Rockwood takes such things so ter- ribly to heart; and you know when I married there was every reason to believe that papa would back us up and help us along, and things have turned out so differently." "Indeed they have, Mrs. Rockwood," said Miss Morgan. "And if your pa knows what is going on here I wonder he can rest in heaven." "I forgive him, I'm sure," said Mrs. Rockwood, "My step-mother poisoned his mind against Mr. Rockwood; and I don't believe he was quite in his right mind when he altered his will and left every- thing to her. If he were living he'd give me this money, if he only knew I needed it, without asking. He never denied me anything," said Mrs. Rock- wood, beginning to weep again. "And she has the homestead and all the property, and an income of at least ten thousand a year, and I am going to be turned out of house and home for five hundred dollars." "Gracious me!" said Miss Morgan. "I don't see how I can go over there and fit her black velvet dress to-morrow. I don't, indeed. I've a good mind to say I won't—there now ?—and have the satisfaction of giving her a piece of my mind to pay for it." "No, no, Miss Morgan. She's a good customer," said Mrs. Rockwood. "It would do me no good. Do you think you can get the waist out, Miss Morgan ?" "I can, by piecing ; and! can make a bit of shell trimming to hide the place," said the dressmaker. Then Mrs. Rockwood went to work on the sew- ing machine. Thankful to have contrived a decent gown without much expenditure of money—linings, buttons, and braid, and Miss Morgan's dollar and a half being all that she could save even by having liver and bacon and codfish dinners twice a week —and the worthy dressmaker stiched away with great diligence, making up her mind that she would say a word for poor Mrs. Rockwood to her step- mother, even if she were snubbed for it. Early next morning MisrMorgan rang the bell at Mrs. Canline's handsome front door, and found the lady ready for her. She always got as much as she could out of people who worked for her, and paid as little for it as possible. There was plenty of the black velvet, however, and of rich lace to trim it with, and the buttons were five dollars a dozen. I•Te skimping and piecing of this elegant costume; and as Miss Morgan stitched she thought of the step-daughter's made-over dress, and inwardly fumed and fretted. How could she get a chance to say anything? And how could she say it SO as to do good, and not harm? "Miss Morgan, I saw you at Mrs. Rockwood's yesterday, didn't I?" said Mrs. Canline, after awhile; and the dressmaker started as though her thoughts could have been read. "Yes, ma'am," she said,- hurriedly. "I went there for a day, to make some old things over, and very hard it was to get one decent dress oht of three, I can tell you. Such a handsome wardrobe as your daughter used to have, too." My daughter? Why, Miss Morgan, you ought not to call Mr. Canline's daughter—a grown young woman when I married him—mine,' said Mrs. Canline, testily. "Dear me! she was engaged to that stupid young Rockwood when I first met poor pa. My daughter ! " "I should have said your step-daughter, Mrs. Canline," said Mrs. Morgan. "But, really, you'd feel sorry to see how hard it is for Is-- - both ends meet." ---- 1, Well, a caarge, I'm sorry," said Mrs. Can- n... .tl3ut, as you make your bed, so you must lie. She offended her pa, and he left her nothing, and me all. I couldn't help that. And I've my dear boy at college just that age that he needs so much money. I told him I should send him a present that was worth while this Christmas. He can't come home—it's too far, you know. And I shall give him five hundred dollars. Of course his expenses are all attended to, but he must have a little swing. There it is all in one note. I shall register it this afternoon." Five hundred dollars ! " said Miss Morgan; exactly the amount of the mortgage the Rock wood's house is to be sold for." "Are they really going to lose their house ? " said the step-mother. "What thriftlessness. Well, I shall send the children a little Christmas present all the same. I shall send them five dol- lars, for I have a silly way of being generous to the undeserving." Miss Morgan bent over her work. "You that have all her father's fortune," she thought—" you who came between parent and child so that he disinherited her. Oh? for shame for shame I" She stitched away, the needle flying through the velvet She fitted the broad shoulders and well. laced waists. She gathered the lace into graceful falls and she thought of Mrs. Rockwood all the h *ile: - It was about four o'clock in the afternoon that Mrs. Canline drew her desk towards, her, and took out two sheets of paper. On one she wrote : "Mir DARLING SON : Here is your Christmas .box. I send it with my best love and wishes. Study hard and make me very proud of you. Yong Mamma." The other sheet held these words "MY Dtme GEORGINA LICIOSed you will find a Cloistmas gift for the children. Spend it carefully. I add this warning, because you are not economical and prudent by nature, you know. Make the best use of it. It is really quite a little sum, when you think of it as yoU should. Affectionately your step- mother r " JANE CANLINE." These two notes lay on the table. Upon the first, a five-hundred dollar note and on the last a humble ftve dollar bill; and Mrs. Canline had carefully directed two envelope.s. When open- ing her paiknife hurriedly, she cut a great gash across her thumb. "Come rind help me, Miss Morgan," she said. "Please put those notes into the envelopes with the money. That for Louis mush be sent to-night I can registop them as. I come froin the doctor's; for the thumb must be seen to. I hate scan on my hands." Miss Morgan ran to the desk, Dent over it; and In a, moment had sealed the notes. Then the lady, slipping them into her pocket, hurried to the doctor's, and was just in time to register her letters at the static,n os the way home. A few days after Mrs.. Canline was hp receipt of two notes, one from her son, whiels ran thus. : "Dear Mamma—Unless you have the queerest possible idea of my wants you must have made a mistake. Did you semi me five dollars? Ye,urs in astonishment.
" Looms CANIIN'E."

The other began: "Dear, kind mamma:- What a. load yen have takea off my heart. That five hundred dollars has saved our home and poor Edward's reason, I be- lieve. Five hundred thousand neverdid mora good. Your ever grateful.step-daughter... "G EORGINA RocKwouri." Mrs. Canline, having read these letters,. eat for while like one petrified. She saw that the money she intended for Louis must hays-gone to. Georgina and vice versa, but it was too late to help it now. She supposed that the pain of her wounded finger had made her stupid. It was clone, as we do most stupid things—in a hurry. Of course she should ' send five other hundreds to Louis. As for Georgina she could not be made to give up.her prize at this date. And Mr. Canline resolved, to play the generous and affectionate parent. She went about for a week or so boasting that she had paid off the mortgag-e on poor Georgina's house; and as Georgina was too 'grateful to hide the fact, Mrs.. CanEne gained a good deal of credit for the kind feeling to. her step-daughter amongst their mutual friends. Many people were surprised; none more so than little Miss Morgan. "I'm so glad," she often said to her thimble. " I did feel so guilty. I really thought / changed • the money in those envelopes. I wanted to do it so. I rejoice that Mrs. Canline did it herself. Ido ; feel gratified she did."

• THE PRETTY GAME OF PLANTIIM—This =us- ing game is played by each person in turn stating that he or she planted something which shall have some connection, ludicrous or otherwise, with what comes up; which latter must be either a tree, a fruit, or a flower :—I planted a Naughty School- boy, and there came up A Birch; A Hasty Marriage, Rue; A Tailor, Cabbage; the Lord Mayor and Corporation' London Pride; A House- maid, Broom ; Parting Lovers, Double Tulips; A learned and beautiful Lady, A Blue Belle; A broken Heart, Love-lies-bleeding; A Forest, A Dandy Lion; A clear Conscience, Heart's Ease; Empty Houses, Lettuce (Let us) ; A Harlequin, Columbine; A pretty Girl, Maidens Blush; A tight Boot, Acorn;. A Spider, Catchfly ; My Heart's Desire, Yew; Cold Weather, Firs; A Merry Christmas, Holly and mistletoe; Absent Friends, Forget me-not • A Clock, Thyme; Anger, Passion-flowers; A Sheep, Phlox; A Donkey, Thistles ; A Negro, Blackberries; An Industrious Woman, Thrift; A Roadside Inn, Travellers' Joy; A Dancing Master, Hops; Chignon, Maiden's Hair; Three per Cents-, Stocks; A Needy Bachelor, Marigold ; Roast Beef, Mustard. MrsTERY.—Two persons must understand the "mystery," which is this :—One person goes out of the room, and another seats four persons in a row, numbering them from left to right, 1,2, 3, 4. The one remaining in the room is to touch one of these four, and the person outside is then admitted, and requested to tell which person was touched. The answer is given through one of the four following signs :—lf No. I was touched, raise your bead and eyes in putting the question to your confederate ; if No. 2, look on the floor; if No. 3, look to the left; and if No. 4, look to the right. AN IMPOSSIBLE PUZZLE. —Ask any one of the party if he could jump over a ruler or a piece of wood when laid on the floor. He will, of course, declare there is nothing so easy. "Easy !" you exclaim, "I will prove it is impossible." You then take the ruler and place it close to the wall.

Mr. Justin McCarthy has gone to Paris to consult Mr. William O'Brien upon the present condition of affairs in Ireland.

The annual tabular statement of the mortality of the Society of Friends shows that whilst the num- ber of deaths during the past year was 15 under five years of age, there were no fewer than 124 who died above 70 years of age.

Some Canndian turkeys have been sent to Lon- don this year. The birds are not so large as natives but have a good flavour and sell well. This is an attempt to find a new market for Canadian produce, now to a large extent closed out of the United States by the operation or the McKinley tariff.

April 5, 1891, has been appointed a Census Day, and the printing machines are already preparing to deliver their cargo of forms. The total number of these which will be required amounts to close on nine millions. A distance of nearly fifteen hundred miles would be covered if sheet by sheet of the forms were placed in a straight line.

Ex-King Milan, of Servia, is once more in London. He is not a striking figure, and his presence here, either recently or now, does not appear to have at- tracted for him any exalted attention. One thing is certain: be will get no invitation to Osborne, for the Queen is known to have in various ways pri- vately shown her sympathy with his divorced consort.

Lord Carrington, late Governor of New South Wales, has been appointed by the Prince of Wales as a member of the Organising Committee of the Imperial Institute. Preparations are being made for the immediate commencement of the erection, to the north of the main building of the institute, of a permanent exhibition gallery of two floors,con- necting those portions of the east and west arcades which are leased to the institute.

Archdeacon Denison's Christmas-box is an an- nouncement that he intends to pursue his purpose of obtaining from Convocation a synodical condem- nation of Mr. Gore for having edited" Lux Mundi." Happily, the archdeacon will be baulked. Opinion in Church circles is not what it was when he did so much to prdouce the Colenso scandal, and Convoca- tion will not be led to define so indefinabe a thing as inspiration.

It appears that Mrs. O'Shea's principal reason for scuttling ,across the water has been to get out of the way of the interviewer. It is an open secret that when at Brighton Mrs. O'Shea was daily pes- tered with requests for interviews and the endless influx of unwelcome applications has at last driven her abroad. It is doubtful whether she will find peace in Paris, for the French have been much in- terested in her case—and the Parisian journalists' are keen interviewers.

One day last week Baron Raimond Franchetti, the father of the composer of "Azrael," who is a millionaire, invited a troop of friends to hunt and fish on his estates at San Gaetano di Caorte, in the province of Venetia. The place was once a marsh, but was reclaimed at great cost by Franchetti, and is now partly pastures, partly cultivated. He is looked upon in the district as the saviour of the people, and is so generous that the peasants live better than anywhere else in Italy.

What with the fog, the frost, the Australian strike, and the general slackness of outdoor work, labourers in the East End, and dock labourers es- pecially, are suffering very severely. Much of the Christmas charity which used to find its way to the East has been diverted by the ratulrtr—nt improve ment in the dockers' condition; but very lin: thought will show how cruelly this process must act when a long spell of slack trade and hitter weather come on. Mr. Mann is urging the forma- tion of municipal workshops as one way out of the difficulty and the London Trades Council are con- sidering his propositions.

I see that Mr. Luis Morgan, who married Lady Rinloss, eldest daughter and heiress of the late Duke of Buckingham, has changed his name for that of Grenville. He had a large assortment to choose from, for his father-in-law was called Richard Plantagent Campbell Temple Brydges Chandoa Grenville, and each of these distinguished names represented a distinct inheritance of blood or land.. Lady Rinloss inherited the Duke's splendid but dismantled palace of Stowe. Ilia adjacent seat of Wotton passed to his nephew, Mr. Gera- Langton, now Lord Temple. Curiously the Duke and his nephew married two sisters, the daughLers of Lady Graham-Montgomery, whose death was recorded on Saturday.

The Romans sent sprigs of holly to their priests as tokens of good wishes. At the heathen festival of Saturnalia houses and temples were decked with evergreens,.but the custom is probably older than the Romans.. Fi'olll the earliest British times the places of worship were decorated with boughs of sweet-smelling plants—such as bay and rosemary I—as well as holly, ivy, box, and other evergreen things; and old writers speak of the market crosses the corners of the streets, the parish churches, and every man's house being decorated with holme or holly, ivy, and bay at Christmas. The idea sug- gested is that of cheerfulness and goodwill to all. A pretty carol of the time of Henry VI praises the holly, and says," The holly has a berry as red as any rose."

Bombay society is much perturbed just now on the subject of whoa is called the "barbarous incon- gruity " of the regulation costume at the Gbver- nor's levees. Lord Reay during his term of office puzzled his friends by desiring them to appear in " a frock coat, or coloured trousers." The disitme- tive particle was painfully ambiguous, and the edict remained, we believe, a dead letter. A recol- lection of this incident, however, has been awakened by an order of Lord Harris prescribing, for what the vulgar call " full fig " at Govern- ment House, " dress coat with white or coloured trousers." The medley does not in the mind's eye look particularly picturesque or dignified, and Bombay spp.ears to be yielding a sullen and sulky sort of obedience which is not far removed from open revolt.

It is not.generally known that the Queen may be claimed by newspaper folk to be the leadiN editor in these realms; but the careful fashion in which she compiles and, when necessary, corrects the official " Court Circular," nightly issued to the press, entitles her to the place. if her sub-editor, who has his offices in London, trips over the slightest word,her Majesty not only promptly takes him up, but lets the whole world know it. On Saturday night, for instance, she caused it to be telegraphed from Osborne that" the statue of the late Emperor Frederick of Germany was unveiled by the Queen on Thursday week immediately before, and not after, the last anthem was sung ix the ser- vice which was performed on the occasion, as it was erroneously stated in the 'Court Circular 'of Friday." There is evidently, in her Majesty's opinion, nothing like accuracy in small details.

The Scotch railway men have struck. That the Christmas traffic, which is much greater in Scot- , land. where the twenty-fifth resembles an English Boxing Day, than in England, will be paralysed, is all owing to the obstinacy of the railway com- panies. They have had two months warning. They were told that unless they conceded the men's r demands—reduced the working hours to ten—there would be a strike in Christmas week. The North Eastern has made just concessions to its employees and averted a similar crisis. Although the officials of the Scotch union were against the strike an over- whelming majority of the men decided to come out. We hope that all railway workers throughout the country will support them. They have legitimate grievances, and a short but firm strike will soon mako the Scotch companies follow the example of the North-Eastern.

. TEN CARDS IN A ClRCLE.—Arrange the spotted cards of any suit (that is from one to ten) in a circular form. Ask a person to think of a number or card, and to touch also ally other number or card ; desire him to add to the number of the card he touched the number of the cards laid out—that is, ten—and then bid him count that sum back- wards, beginning at the card he touched, and reckoning that card at the number he thought of; by counting thus he will end it at the card or number he nrst thought of, and thereby enable you to ascertain what that was. For example, suppose he thought of the number three, and touched the sixth card, if ten be added to six, it will of course make sixteen ; and if he counts that number from the sixth card, the one touched, in a retrograde order, reckoning three on the sixth, four on the fifth, five on the fourth, six on the third cards, and so pn, it will be found to terminate on the third card, which will, therefore, show you the number the person thought of. When the person is counting the numbers, he should not, of course, call them out aloud.

A FRENcR MAYOR, who at one time held the office of stipendiary magistrate, was about to perform the civil rite, of marriage. " Mademoiselle X—," he said, addressing the bride, " Do you agree to take Mr. Z-- here present for your wedded hus- band?" And, after the young lady had replied in the affirmative, the Mayor, turning to the bride- groom, delivered himself as follows : "Prisoner at the bar, what have you to say in your defence ?"

A BERLIN Junoa, the other day, whet:addressing a locksmith who appeared aa witness, spoke as follows: "I should have thought you would ' dissuade your workmen from going to law for such la trifle !' Witness : "That's what I did. I said: 'Children, said I, 'the' clerk, at the lawyers will take your coat, and the lawyer will strip off your shirt, and as for the Judge, why, men,, he'll skin you alive You see, I talked sensibly to the folks like that, but it waS all no use !" • " an bland in the Blei Fjord," says Mr. E. F. Knight, "is exclusively inhabited by fishermen who form a race apart. They keep up the customs of their forefathers, speak in Danish, and will not intermarry with the mainland people. There are only feur or five surnames among them, and as the Christian names deemed by hem orthodox are also limited in number, it comes that many people have the same names, and so have to be distinguished by nicknames expressive of some personal or other quality. For instance, there are thirty Peter Masses there; and I saw a letter addressed to one- in which. he was described as, He that is the elder of the two Peter Masses that have red hair.' The duties of the Mmsholm post- man must be arduous and sometimes delicate. A STORY has been recently related in the French papers of " the Saucy," which is one of the his- toric diamonds of the world. Jules Janin, the well-known French. critic, it appears, was one day visiting the Louvre in company -with the Princess Demidoff. The Princess,. -finding the weather warm, laosened her shawl, which she held by a brooch containing the famous diamond. This she handed to Janiu to keep, who in the midst of an animated discussion slipped the jewel hastily into his. waiscoat pocket, he and the Princess entirely forgetting the matter. On the morrow however, the loss was noticed and Janin, in 'a fever of excitement, con- fessed his utter inability to state what, he had done with , the brooch. Ransacking his clothes he suddenly remembered he had put the jewel into the pocket of the white waistcoat he was wearing. "That," coolly replied his servant, "went? .thi! morning to the wash." It required some tact to further trace a jewel worth it may be mentioned, smile sixty or seventy thousand pounds. Fortu- nately the worthy laundress confessed she had regarded the brooch as no value, and had given it to her little boy to play with, and in the hands of the little fellow' it was founci. To his' dying day, Janin was wont to say he never related theilstory without a shudar.

IT has long been known that in some specirness of bamboo a ronnd stone is found at the joints of the cane. This is called " tabasheer," and is supposed . .

to be deposited from the silicious. juices of thane. Another curiosity of the sort is the "cocoanut stone," found in the endosperm of tha cocoanut in Java and other East India islands. It is, accord- ing to Dr. Kincunins, a is;re carbonate of lime ; and the shape of the stone is sometimes round, some- times pear shaped, while the appearanca is that of pearl without much lustre. Some of tho stones are as large as cherries, and as hard as felspar or opal. They are very rarely fount. and are regiarded as precious stones by Oriental, and charms against; disease or evil spirits by the Datives.

Beautiful are tlglly im life, these winter roses, and in death they shall not be divided; when Death comes, he will pluck,, not one, but both.—Altzunder Smut " T87321E sheets in the wind' means unsteady from drinking, just as a ship is unsteady when its sheets are in the wind. The sail of a ship is fastened at one of the bottom corners by a rope called a "tack," the other corner is left more or less free as the rope called a " sheet " is dispossd ; if quite free the sheet is said to be "in the wind," and the sail flaps and flutters without restraints If the three sails were so loosened the ship would. reel and stagger like a drunken inZta. He may be correct in his calculation, but it would be extremely difficult to. assemble that many people together for the purpose of making the test. People who clasp hands haw a way of :locking off by themselves in couples, holding that thirty-two millions is no company.

Two monks were once outvying, each other in, bidding for an abbey, when William Rufus, who was King at the time noticed a third at some dis- tance who never said a word. The King asked .why he did not make an offer like the others; the, monk eai/.1 be was poor, and. hesides, would ghre nothing if he were ever so rich. "Then," replied the King, "-jou are the fittest person to have it," and immediately gave it hira. Shortly after that date small parcela"of tea, valued at £lO sterling per pound, were imported frem China to the East Indies, whence they made their way to London as presents to son-...e of its wealthy citizens, The first large con3ignment of tea was received in 1657 by Thomas Garway, a London merchant, and with it he opened "a stand," kii.,,•vn in our times as " Garraway's Coffoe.House," :!:n the sale, not of coffee, but of tea. NAPOLEON AFTER WATERLoo.—Whether any course was open to Napoleon after the disaster of Waterloo other than that which he adopted, a second abdication, is certainly very doubtful. Had he taken the precaution to dissolve the Chambers before setting out on the campaign, he probably could have rallied the nation and protracted the struggle. But the Chambers were unfriendly; any Parliamentary body is naturally unfriendly to a military despotism; and, at that juncture, nothing less than a military despotism could possibly have saved France from the calamity of the restoration of the Bourbons by foreign bayonets. Hence, unless Napoleon shoulol execute a new coup d'dtat, there was nothing for him but abdication. On the 15th of July, 1815, Napoleon surrendered himself on board the British man-of-war Bellerophon. Of his appearance and bodily condition during the two months of his stay on this vessel we have an interesting account in the narrative of Captain Maitland, who commanded the ship. Maitland describes him as a remarkably strong, well-built man, about sft. 7in. high, his limbs particularly well formed, with a fine anklo and very small foot, of which he seemed rather vain, as he always wore, while on board the ship, silk stockings and shoes. His hands were also very small, and had the plumpness of a woman's rather than the robustness of a man's. His eyes, light grey •, teeth good; and when he smiled, the expression of his countenance was highly pleasing; when under the influence of disappointment. •however, it assumed a dark, gloomy cast. His hair was of very dark brown, nearly approaching black, and, though a little thin on the top and front, had not a grey hair amongst it. His complexion was a very uncommon one, being of a light, sallow colour, diffaring from almost any other I ever met with. From his hav- ing been corpulent, he had lost much of his person- al activity, and if we are to give credit to those who attended him, a very considerable portion of his mental energy was also gone. It is certain his habits were very lethargic while he was on board the Bellerophon; for though he went to bed at eight or nine o'clock in the evening, and did not rise till about the same hour in the morning, he frequently fell asleep on the sofa in the course of the day. His general appearance was that of a man • rather older than he then was. —From Scribner'B Magazine. •

GYMNASTICS AT Scnooie —The honorary secretary of the National Physical Recreation Society gave some interesting evidence lately before the Royal Commission on Elementary Education, and it had the advantage over much of the other matter collected by that body of being statistical in large measure. Speaking of the work done by the Liverpool Gymnasium for the treatment of spinal curvature, he stated that some 3,000 cases had come under his own observation there of which 2,500 were cases of children between die ages of eight and fcurteen years, 2,000 of these being girls. There can be no doubt, we think, that deficient physical exercise, if not the only or even perhaps chief cause of this very common deformity, is highly calculated to promote it; and, even apart from any specific evil, a well-considered and sys- tematised plan of training for the muscles is un- doubtedly a most valuable regimen, and eminently adapted to preserve and benefit the general health. But it is of the highest importance, in following out this observation, to avoid pernicious exercises, which may do irreparable mischief to the growing organs and unbraced body of a child. The follow- ing instance is very much in point:—" The care- taker commanded them all (like children of an ele- mentary school) to keep their knees stiff and touch their toes with their hands, and while he kept them in that position he proceeded to give them an im- promptu discourse upon the benefit of physical training. div.p: THE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW; OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
BY SYLVA.NTJS COBB, JR.
CHAPTER X.

A STRANGE DISCOVERY. The news went out that the Count Conrad Dam- onoff must die. A few days before the best surgeon in Moscow said he would recover; but now that same surgeon said he must fall. A strange change had come over him. It was not a fever, but rather a consuming of vitality. He was failing fast, and no art of medicine could revive him. Some thought he must be bleeding inwardly, but others knew bet- ter than this, because in that case there would be some outward symptom. The wound itself was healing, but the disease was not. The physician and the priests were now in daily, and the former almost in hourly, attendance. The surgeon was Ropani ; and the priest was the hump-backed Savotano. Thus lay the count on his bed, weak, and faint, but at present almost free from pain, and an old woman was his only attendant, the priest having just left. It was just after noon. The dying man had just taken a powerful stimulating draught, though it was against the injunctions of the priest, as he said that by such means the invalid might die bereft of sense, and thus lose his hold upon salva- tion—he had just taken his draught when there was a low rap at the door. The woman arose to answer the summons. She conversed a few mo- ments with the girl who had knocked, and when she returned to the bed she announced that Ruric Nevel wished to enter.
" Let him come in," whispered the count. "But—"

_ "Never mind," he interrupted, its the woman commenced thus to expostulate. " Let him come in. By heavens, if he is my enemy let me see him. It may serve to arouse me." So the woman went to the door again, and soon afterwards Rune Pievel entered the apaitment. He stepped lightly, noiselessly, to the bedside, but it was some moments ere he could distinguish objects by the subdued light of the place. By and by, however, he overcame the diffiulty, and he started back in horror as he beheld the features of his ad- versary. How pale and sunken ! How deathlike and ghastly ! The count noticed the movement, ane he noticed the look. "Count Damonoff," spoke the gun-maker, in a low, solemn tone, " a few days since I heard that you were recovering, and I thanked God. But to- day they told me you were dying, and I have come to ask that I may take your hand ere you pass away from earth. As God is my Maker and my Judge, I would rather lie down here and die fur you than have you pass away with a curse of me upon your soul or on your lips. Forgive me for what I have done, and never again will I engage in such a wicked work. For my own life, it is my country's and my mother's, and I have no right to throw it away ; and my antagonist's life is the sacred property of God, which I have no right to touch but in self- defence. Forgive me." Slowly and heavily moved the dying man over, and then he extended his thin and wasted hand. " Ruric," he said—and his voice was stronger now, for the potion was working—" I am glad you have come—very glad ; for I have wished, above all else of earth, to see you. I could not send for you, fJr I knew not how you might come. I have been all wrong in the things that have passed betwixt thee and me. I was mad, and a fool. I blame you not ; but rather do I thank you for your kindness through all the scene. Oh, I forgive you with all my heart; and now tell me that I am forgiven I" "Forgiven ?" repeated Ruric,with a trembling lip, till holding the count's hand within both his own. utd to nod Izofid call you back to life! Forgiven? Oh, God, who-r-ans—air-ben-re.,-I.3za_ how humble, how sacred, is my forgiveness to you! Could I call you back—could I wipe out the past from my memory, I could die content." "Enough," returned the count warmly. "This was my holiest wish, though pride has kept back its utterance. Oh, I feared you would gloat over my death—that you would be glad when, I was gone !" "No, no; I should have been a monster then." "There are many such. And yet I wronged you by the thought. But I could not help it." A moment more passed in silence, and then the invalid resumed:
;11 'Olruj&thJfld

"There is one reason why I should like•to live ; I should be prepared for a better life. Since death has come—since I have known that he stood wait- ing by my bed —I have wondered at the evil life I have led ; and I have thought that if the dark king would let me remain here a few years more I could be a better man. But 'tis too late now. The die is cast. Yet I have some joy in this. You have shed a happy light upon my dying hour. God bless you." Rune's feelings were easily moved, and there was something in the deep solemnity of this occasion that started his heart to a tender mood ; and the last words of the dying man flowed the cup. He bowed his head, and covering his eyes with one hand,while he held in the other the hand of Conrad, he wept freely and silently. At this moment the woman arose and left the LOOM. "She's gone," said the count, after be had re- covered somewhat from the deep emotions which had been stirred within his own soul. "Sit down here beside me." Runic obeyed the request, and after he had I stated himself he gazed sadly into the sick man's face. "Say, Ruric," the Count- asked, while an eager look overspread his face, " was't true what Ropani told me ; that you overcame Demetnus the Greek with the sword ?" " I did," the youth replied, in a whisper. "But you did not disarm him 2—you did rot fairly take his sword from him ?" " I did, Conrad." "My soul, is it possible? And where have you been all your life ?" " In Moscow, and in Spain." "And yet obscure." -"Never mind that now," interposed Ruric. "I have something of more interest. Do you—but you will pardon me for what I may say, for I assure you I mean it all for your good." "Speak on," said Conrad, at the same time run- ning his eyes almost enviously over the gunmakera' nobly-developed breast and shoulders. "Then, first—l have just come from the lady Rosalind—Ah—l meant not—" "Go on. I may have felt a pang at the mention of that name, but I know she loves you, and were I strong at thi3 moment as ever I'd relinquish all claims of her to you. So fear not." " Thank you, Sir Count, for this—but I was re- marking: lam not long from her presence, and between us both we have suspected some dark things. Do you think the duke was really your friend ?" The Count started, and a strange gleam shot from his eyes. " Go on," he uttered. 'Then listen : Before you ever came to my shop the duke had solemnly promised Rosalind that she should receive no more trouble from you—that you would claim her hand no more," " Do you know this ?" "I do." "But it cannot be. Why should he have sent me on that mission to you 2" "I had taught one of his officers the sword exer- cise, and he knew I was your superior in strength and the use of the weapon." "Well— go on !" whispered the count, nervously and anxiously. "Why—he thought very likely that we should I not meet on such a question without a quarrel. He r knew your natural impetuosity, and my strength of arm, and hoped you—would fall." " But—go on !" "his estate is running out and he wants the whole of Drotzen !" " Ah ! I see it now !" "The duke had proposed himself for Rosalind's hand," resumed Rune. "He says he has loved her long; and he will force her to marry him if he can, though he breaks her heart !" "My God !" gasped the count, fairly starting up to a sitting posture ; "how blind I have been! By my soul, he never was cordial—never kind." Rune gently laid the sick man back, and then he said: "From all I can see and understand, the proud duke meant to get all your wealth and all of Rosa- hi'nd's." The count spoke not yet. He lay with his eyes closed, and groaned in agony at the strange revela- tions that were breaking in upon him. But see ! Why starts Rune so suddenly ?—and why does he turn so pale? Why do his hands trem- ble ?—and why is his brow bent so eagerly " What is it 2" asked the count startled by the strange event. "fold !" whispered Runic in a frantic tone. " ou were recovering once ?"
"From this wound ?" "Yes."
"Yes. I was getting well fast, and the doctors Lid I should be stout and well in a month. But . _ .

suddenly this change eame on. Let's see—on Fri- day morning I felt the first relapse." "The very time !" gasped Ruric to himself. The count moved his head forward, and would have caught his companion by the hand if he could. "For God's sake, Ruric, what is it ?" "As I came this way I saw a humpbacked priest pass out from this house ?" said the gun-maker interrogatively. "Yes—yes," returned the count, speaking shortly and quickly. "It was Savotano. He has attended me. The Duke recommended him." . . _

"And was he here Thursday night ?" " Thursday ? Ah—yes—he watched with me that night." "And has he been in attendance since ?" " Ye.s ; every day. But why do you ask? Say— what is that meaning upon your face? What is it? At this moment the door of the apartment was quietly, noiselessly opened, and Kopani, the sur- geon, entered the place. " Ha!" cried Runic Starting towards him, and grasping him by the arm," your patient is poisoned r A deadly poison has been given him, and it is even now eating his life away !" "Impossible !" gasped the surgeon, straining his eyes to see plainly who it was that spoke to him. " Ah," he uttered, as he became somewhat used to the gloom of the apartment, "is it you, sir ?" "Aye—but mind now that now. Cannot you do something for the count? He has been poisoned." "It cannot be !"

"By the hopes of my salvation !" cried Conrad Damonoff, starting up to a sitting posture, "he speaks the truth! That accursed priest !—Oh Olga! Olga! lnever dreamed that thou wast mine enemy!" "But what is it all 2" the surgeon asked, gazing first upon Runic, and then upon the count. "Speak. some one."

"Tell him," groaned Conrad. " Listen :" said the gun-maker. "I have my sus- picions, but mind you, they are founded on facts, and the facts are these: The Duke of Tula is well- nigh free from the possession of property. His half of Drotzen is all mortgaged, and he wants the other half. That other half he cannot have while Damon- off lives. The duke, too, has sworn that Rosalind Valdai shall be his wife—so he would have her pro- perty, also. This humpbacked priest is Olga's special tool. It was Olga got him into the church, and it was Olga who freed him more than once trom deserved punishment. Last Thursday evening he was with the duke in private council, and he came from thence directly to this place. Now you can judge for yourself.' The surgeon started slightly, and then he bowed his head. A few moments he remained thus, and then he leaped up and clasped his hands. "By the Living God of all things," he cried, "it is! it is! There is no burning up, as I thought, of icy, wintry fire; but the hellish work is from a human hand! Hold !—I know the symptoms. I know them now. Be quiet, Conrad. It may not yet be too late." As the surgeon spoke he hastily opened a small leathern case he carried with him, and from thence he took a powerful emetic. The woman was sent for, and when she came she obtained warm water. The potion was given a small quantity at a time— at intervals of about five minutes, until the desired effect was produced. A strange mass of stuff was thrown up, and Kopani took it to the light and ex- amined it. Most of it was of dark, brownish color, but with streaks of yellow, and coarse blotches of red and green. The yellow substance was of a muc- ous formation; while the 'red and green seemed to be more liquid. "'Tis poison !" the surgeon said; "and it has been • . . • .

administered in small quantities." "And cannot something be done ?" asked Ruric, erip-'6•011, save him if you can! Save him and I'll bless you ever. You can—oh, say you can !" The surgeon caught the youth by the hand. There was something in this noble spirit that moved him —and he knew now that all must have been for- given between the two men. " I'll try," he said, "I have antidotes with me. By heavens, all is not lost yet." "Then hasten," urged Runic, half crazed beneath the weiAht of the great discovery which he had thus helped to make. "Be not uneasy. I will see that he suffers not for want of human skill." And as the surgeon thus spoke he moved to the sideboaru 'and mixed an antidote; bnt he did not give it until the invalid had vomited all he could. "Hold ! "cried Runic, as the surgeon took up the wine to mix the antidote with. " Touch not a thing here. Perhaps the villain has poisoned them all ! "

"So it may be," Kopani said, setting down the bottle. He then turned to the woman, who had re- mained standing by the like one in a trance, and asked her to bring a fresh bottle of wine. She quickly obeyed, and when she was gone Kopani took all the articks upon the table and set them on one side. He would not throw them away, for ha meant to analyze them. When the woman returned Kopani mixed the new portion, and administered it, and ere long after- wards the count fell asleep. "Rune Nevel," said the surgeon, as soon as he was sure the invalid would sleep, " will you remain here awhile? I wish to go and analyze some of these things. I have only to go to the Academy. I will be back again man hour at the furthest." The gun-maker gladly consented to this; and having gathered up the phials and,,the wine-bottle. and concealed them beneath his pelisse, the sur- geon left. Runic Nerel was happier now, tor hope was with him while he prayed that Gcd might spare the un- fortunate count.
(To be continued.)

THE SEVERE WEATHER. ' SEVERAL PERSONS FROZEN TO DEATH. DELAY OF TRAFFIC. Dense fog has prevailed at Liverpool, and the incon- venience to shipping has been great. Several mail steamers which should have sailed on Saturday only left on Monday morning, taking: advantage of a slight lift in the fog. These steamers included the Cunard liner, Umbria, the Guion steamer Wisconsin, the West India steamer Bernard Hall, and others, while other steamers wereunable to get out. The inward boats having been similarly delayed. Just outside the Alexandra entrance there were quite a fleet of steamers at anchor. They could not get into the dock, although the distance was but a few yards. During the fog on Saturday and Sunday the steamer traffic to the Isle of Man was seriously impeded. The Fenella left Douglas on Saturdaymorning at nine o'clock, and made slow progress across the Channel. She had to anchor in the Mersey with her passengers all night, and did not arrive in Liverpool until Sunday at noon, the passage having occupied about 28 hours. Much incon- venience was caused on account of the non-arrival of letters and newspapers. A ghastly discovery was made early on Sunday morn- ing in Ruby-street, Toxteth Park, Liverpool, when the body of a man unknown was found. The man, who is believed to have been frozen to death, was about 35 Tears of age, 51t. 6in. in height, of light complexion,and with brown moustache. Ile had a scar wound over the left eyebrow, upon which was a piece of sticking-plas- ter. The dress he wore was a dark brown overcoat, tweed jacket and vest, black and white stripe pants, grey socks, and lace-up-boots. In his pockets there were found £.2 17s. 6d., a steel punch, and a key. Thomas Blackburn, an old man, has been found froten to death at a short distance from his own house at Cop- penhall, near Stafford. The river Dee on Monday was frozen over from Ches- ter to Eaton Hall, a run of five and a half miles. A Reuter's telegram from Toulon says :—A fearful storm has been raging here to-day (Monday), and a great many shins have been forced to take refuge in the har- bour. The brig Leoine, of Marseilles, has foundered in the storm, and five of the crew of seven men were

drowned. On Monday the steamer Orator, of Liverpool, bound from Greenock to Sicily with a cargo of coal, struck during the fog on Briggs Reef, county Down, and be- came a wreck. The crew, numbering 20, got away in the ship's boats, and after obtaining shelter at the coast- guard station proceeded to the Sailors' Home in Belfast. KITCHEN BOILER EXPLOSION NEAR LIVERPOOL. TWO LIVES LOST AND TWO PERSONS INJURED. An explosion of a kitchen boiler, unhappily attended by fatal results, occurred on Sunday evening at Tue- brook. The house in which the explosion took place was 17, March-road, one of a series of dwelling-houses which have been erected within the last ten years, and which contain a boiler supplying hot water to the bath- room upon the upper floor. At this house there resided Mr. William Sumner, a commercial traveller.; his wife, Liatie Sumner, aged,twenty-five ; their child. Maud, a girl five years of age; and a niece of Mr. Sumner, Ellen Maddocks aged nine years. The four people mentioned were seated at tea in the kitchen at six o'clock on Sun- day night, when the boiler exploded, with the result that Mrs. Sumner and her daughter were killed, while Mr Sumner and his niece were badly scalded, the former sustaining injuries about the neck, face, and legs, and the latter upon the face and arms. The first intimation of the explosion was given to Sergeant Pitt, at Tuebrook Station, by Mr. Furniss, chemist, of Rocky-lane ; and Inspector Hinds, accompanied by Sergeant Pitt, immedi- ately went to the house. Here they found the place in a state of the greatest confusion. The boiler in the back kitchen and the fire range had been completely blown away, and lay in the middle of the floor, while the force of the explosion was so great that the back door, the window, and the back of the grate were also blown out, the kitchen being a complete wreck. Dr. Edwards, of Rocky-lane, was called in, and he at once rendered as- sistance to the sufferers, but both mother and child died within half an hour after the explosion. It appears that they were struck by flying portions of the iron of the boiler or of the masonry. Both Mr. Summer and his niece declined to be removed, and the latter was taken to the house of a neighbour, where she was attended to. The cause of the accident was that the cistern-pipe which supplied the boiler with water became fromen, and the water remaining in the boiler generated the steam ,which resulted in the explosion. Several boiler explosions took place on Sunday of a minor character, but by these there was neither loss of life nor injury inflicted. It was ascertanied on Monday afternoon that three explosions of kitchen boilers, in addition to the disas- trous one at Anfield, had taken place in the vicinity of Liverpool on Sunday night. One was in Paterson-st., Birkenhead ; another at 236, West-Derby-road, Liver- pool, and a third at 97, Bell-road, Seacombe. A copper cylinder also exploded at 3, Eastbourne-road, West, Birkdale, with disastrous results to the building. At Birkdale, on Tuesday, a serious explosion occurred at the house occupied by Mrs_ Hazleden, in Albert-road. The kitchen boiler burst, blew out the fireplace and the kitchen window, and demolished the dining-room wall. An old servant was seriously injured. HOUSEHOLD BOILER EXPLOSIONS. Mr. Wm. Ingham, M. I. Mech. E., writes as follows from Moston to the editor of the Manchester "Examiner and Times :"—As the season of the year is at hand when these distressing occurrences become more frequent, it has struck me that a few extracts from my small shilling pamphlet on "Household Boiler Explosions," giving simple instructions on how to secure safety during frost, might prove acceptable and useful to many of your readers who simply exist in terror during the continu- ance of a severe frost. It cannot be too widely known that there is no necessity for any alarm if people will only take the trouble to know how their hot-watersystems are arranged, and adopt a few simple precautions to avoid risk. Many persons, should the water supply hap- pen to beeorne frozen, dare not keep a fire in the kitchen grate, as they conclude the boiler will become red hot for want of water and explode. I have numbers of let- ters from people who, with this idea, will not light their kitchen fires, and who thus put themselves to great and unnecessary inconvenience during a prolonged frost. 1/111 this is unnecessary, as safety can be ensured at all times by the adoption of a few common-sense precautions, and the following instructions have been drawn up in such a manner as to be easily understood by any person of ordinary intelligence. DURING FROST, keep the kitchen fire burning day and night, and close the damper after" banking" or "raking" the fire for the night. Frequently test the hot-water taps, both in scullery and bathroom, especially last thing at night and first thing in the morning. If nothing but steam issues from the hot-water taps leave one tap open. THERE IS NO DANGER if warm water can be dravin freely at any one of the hot-water taps, and rarely if water be found to flow freely at one of these taps, even if cold; when there are two cisterns, sc long as the water in one is found to be warm ; under any circumstances, where a reliable safety valve is attached direct to the boiler. THERE IS DANGER only where there is no reliable safety valve or other safeguard attached to the boiler, and when all commu- nication between the boiler and external air is closed, either by the pipes leading to and from the boiler or cylinder becoming choked with ice, or by closing of stop-cocks &c. During the Christmas and New Year holidays families frequently leave home and lock up their houses for several days. It is at such times as these, when there is no fire in the house for several days, that everything becomes frozen up, and on the return of a family, when I a fire is lighted, there being no communication between the boiler and the supply cistern or the external air, pressure accumulates in the boiler behind the kitchen fire until the vessel explodes. It is notthat the boiler be- comes red hot, as it is so generally believed, but simply that steam is generated which :has no means of escape, and pressure thus accumulates which ultimately ruptures
the boiler.

SERIOUS ALLEGATIONS AND DENIALS. DETROIT, MONDAY.—A nun who had run away from the House of the Good Shepherd because of difficulties between her and the mother superior was discovered yesterday at the residence of some friends, but she re- fused to return to the convent, alleging that gross cruelties had been practised upon her. She says that the tasks given to the nuns were extrenaely onerous ,and frequently impossible to perform in the allotted time, which results M the delinquents being whipped with a strap. She states that one sister died while being -whipped, and another died from bad food given to the nuns. The mother superior denies charges of the escaped nun. Bishop Foley says he believes them to be untrue.

div.head: KILKENNY ELECTION.
div.p: THE KILKENNY ELECTION.
---- DEFEAT OF THE PA.RNELLITE.

GREAT NATIONALIST MAJORITY. The Parnellites on Saturday mostly confined their efforts to busily canvassing in North Kilkenny ; and as regards the other side, Mr. M'Carthy and Mr. Sexton have left the district. The medical men in attendance on Mr. Parnell have issued a written declaration adher- ing to their statement that the substance thrown into his eyes was lime. The ladies of Kilkenny, on Satur- day, waited upon Mr. Parnell, and presented him with a bouquet of flowers and an address, in which they complimented him on the pluck displayed during the contest, and expressed disgust at the language of his opponents. Mr. Parnell yesterday went out to Clara and Johnswell. At the former place Father Walsh and Sir Thomas Esmonde were holding an opposition meeting, and after some parley the member for Cork made a brief speech. At Johnswell there was a much larger gather- ing. Mr. Parnell said that Grattan would have won Ireland's legislative independence, but he forgot that he had a treacherous English foe, who knew how to use the dagger and poisoned bowl of diplomacy. The dis- bandment of the Volunteers of 1782 lost Ireland her free- dom. He expressed his determination not to give in, even if Kilkenny went against him, until every Irish constituency had been tested. Mr. T. Harrington, who had just arrived from America, also spoke during the day on Mr. Parnell's behalf. POLLING. Polling for North Kilkenny took place on Monday at fifteen stations in various parts of the constituency. Elaborate police and military preparations were made in view of possible disturbances, but everything went off quietly, and there was no collision. In Kilkenny City a protest was lodged on behalf of the Parnellite candidate against priests being allowed in the precincts of the courthouse, and the returning officer ordered that no one should be permitted to enter the gates but voters and those having business in the building. At Castlecomer the voters came up in contingents, usually, headed by priests, and at one point an alter- cationtook place between Mr. T. Harrington and the rev, gentlemen in reference to alleged interference with electors. In this division the personating agents were all priests. At Gowran, which was relied upon by the Far- nellites to counteract the hostile vote at Castlecomer, the proceedings passed off quietly, and a majority of the electors on the register had polled before three o'clock. Mr. Parnell drove round the constituency during the day, visiting first Gowran, and then 'proceeding via Kilkenny to Freshford. He seemed in excellent spirits, but at the Parnellite headquarters in Kilkenny City there were dismal forebodings of the result.
THE RESULT. The result of the polling was declared on Tuesday after- noon, as follows : Hennessy 2,527 Scully 1,365

Majority for Hennessy... 1,162 A lezge crowd assembled in front of the courthouse at Kilkenny, where the counting took place, and the persons present being chiefly supporters of Mr. Parnell,there were some rather unpleasant scenes when prominent mem- bers of the victorious party made their appearance. On leaving the courthouse Mr. Parnell was hoisted shoulder high, and loudly cheered. Mr. Tim Healey left the build- ing by the back way, but was detected by the mob, who started in hot pursuit, and the Sub-sheriff who was with the hon member, had to appeal for police protection. Mr. Healey was bespattered with mud, after which about forty constables got around him and escorted him and his brother, Mr. Maurice Healey, to their hotel. Addressing the crowd, Mr. Parnell said there was a conspiracy against him which was originated by Mr. Davitt and Mr. Stead, who having failed to destroy the Home Rule Bill, pretended to be its friend in order that by gaining admission to the Home Rule ranks they might strike a deadly blow from the rear. He did not regard as more than a feather the pat on the cheek that the northern division of Kilkenny had given him, rather in petulance than in anger, but, strengthened by the repulse, he should press forward in every Irish con- stituency, and he was confident as to the result. He repeated his declaration that if the constitutional struggle became useless he would take the advice of the people and be guided by their judgment. All accounts agree that the return of Sir J. Pope Hennessy was looked for on both sides, and that it was only the extent of the majority which caused sur- prise.

PETITION AND LIBEL ACTION. The special correspondent of the Press Association learns that a petition against the return of Sir John Pope Hennessy will be at once lodged on behalf of Mr.Vineent Scully, the grounds being—undue interference with the voters by the priests, especially at Castlecomer and Ballyragget. In those two places the peisonating agents for Sir J. Pope Hennessy were priests, and it is alleged that their interference was unduly exercised in the case of illiterate voters. Dr. Tanner states that he shall institute legal proceed- ings against Mr. Parnell fcr alleged libel contained in a speech delivered from the windows of the Victoria Hotel on Saturday evening last. THE NATIONAL COMMITTEE. The first public meeting of the National Committee , elected to support the action of the majority of the Irish Parliamentary party was held at Dublin on Monday. Mr. Murphy, M.P., who presided, said the fact that Mr. Parnell had anticipated his defeat in Kilkenny was clear from his announcement that from that county he would carry the light into every Irish constituency. In face of that declaration the National Committee must be for a time a committee of public safety to meet Mr. Parnell in his mad career and use every legitimate means to stop him. The necessity for the formation of the National Committee became evident when they saw that the National organizations were all being worked in the interest of Mr. Parnell. He described the steps taken to counteract the influence which had been brought to bear in journalism in favour of Mr. Parnell, and proceeded to state what was intended to be done towards a reorganiz- ation of the National League. Mr. Thomas Dickson, M.P., spoke of the Kilkenny election as a magnificent victory for Home Rule. Mr. Parnell, he said, had—instead of making some reparation to outraged public opinion—followed his own personal ambition, and was nst afraid or ashamed to shipwreck the cause for which he had done so much. There could be no compromise. They would never again follow the leadership of Mr. Parnell. Other members spoke, including Mr. Swift McNeill, who said that all Ireland would ef.dorse the verdict of Kilkenny. MR. McCARTHY'S OPINION. Mr. Justin M`Carthy. M.P., told a news agency's re- presentative at Boulogne on Tuesday that he thonght the result of the Kilkenny election was an indication of the anti-Parnellite feeling throughout Ireland. He.did not think Mr. Parnell would desire to contest another constituency, for North Kilkenny was one of the worst divisions in the country for the anti-Parnellites to fight. THE INSUPPRESIBLE. At Dublin, on Tuesday, two men were committed for trial for abandoning " Insuppressible," the new news- paper started by the anti-Parnellites. The defendants asserted that when in charge of a cart taking parcels of the paper to Kingsbridge s:ation, they were Set upon by a body of men, who compelled them to go to Phcerdx Park and throw their load away. The prosecution alleged that the men had been bribed to get rid of the

papers. ARRIVAL OF MR. PARNELL IN LONDON. Mr. Parnell on Wednesday night left Kingstown by the Irish mail for London, where he arrived at half-past seven o'clock on Thursday morning. He wore a bandage over one of his oyes, looked very fatigued and haggard, and travelled quite alone. He said to a reporter that he would meet Mr. O'Brien in Paris, but declined to say anything as to the prospects of the forthcoming negotiations. On his return from Paris, Mr. Parnell will rest for a few days in London, and begin his campaign in Ireland early in the new year, opening at Limerick and Waterford. MR. W. O'BRIEN IN PARIS. Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., arrived at Boulogne on Thursday forenoon, by the steamer Obdam, from New York. In the afternoon Mr. O'Brien had a conference with Mr. Justin M'Carthy, M.P., Mr. Condon, M.P., Mr. Sexton, M.P., and Father Humphreys, but no decision was come to regarding future action. Mr. O'Brien, who was in good health, expressed himself delighted with the result of the North Kilkenny election, but declined to say anything on the general situation. Mr. O'Brien was also seen by the editor of the " Freeman's Journal," who is understood to have been sent to explain to the hon. member the Parnellite view of the situation.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 27, 1890. I EXECUTION OF MRS. PIERCY. I
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 27, 1890. I EXECUTION OF MRS. PIERCY. I
THE TIED HOUSES SYSTEM. We take the following extracts from a special 'aper on Tied louses in the "Manchester Guar-

din." "Tied houses" is the name now commonly ap- plied to inns and other places for the retailing of intoxicants in which brewers and wholesale dealers have acquired the control of all supplies. They have even gone further, and by assuming the whole management, as vested in the license-holder have created a vast network of public-houses, abso- lutely controlled by the brewer. This system of tied houses is of comparatively recent adoption. Five- and-twenty years ago, except in some country and market towns where the principal inns were sup- plied with beers from their own breWeries,there was nothing which could compare to the present great monopoly. But when the brewer had thoroughly grasped the possibilities of the licensing system he set about the work of public-house amalgamation in I a Napoleon-like way. Although the Legislature Ihad prescribed no limitation as to the number of public-houses, it had become plain that the magis- trates generally had determined that no great in- crease would be permitted. With increasing national wealth, as well as a rapidly-growing population, the values of licensed houses, it was plain, must go higher. At first the monopoly aimed at was simply beer. Spirits were then added. Tobacco followed. "Mineral waters "—a growing demand—came next. There was yet a void. With a bona-fide tenant of the house, even though tha sources of supply were not free, actual sales must be made, a discount given; a margin of profit, which could be made available for the brewer-holder went to the license- holder. The discovery followed that the Licensing Acts did not beyond all possibility of escape pro- vide that a public-house should be tenanted by that license-holder who was amenable to the law. Thus it was possible to displace the tenant by a servant of the brewery, a clerk, a manager, any person adapted to the trade who could, at a sufficiently small salary, deal out without murmur the articles supplied and return the profit in full. The accom- plishment of this end completed the "tied house " system. So quickly has it grown that out of the 104,000 licensed houses which now supply he English pub- lic with liquor in its various kinds it is believed that scarcely more than the odd 4,000 are absolutely free. In Manchester there are 2,575 licensed houses of all kinds. Beershops with " on" licences—num- bering I,3lB—form the majority of these. There is 1 scarcely a beerhouse in Manchester that is free. Seventy-two houses in Manchester are registered as I belonging to one firm; another has some sixty-seven to its credit ; another nearly fifty, and so on. These, added to the houses tied either by lease or by agree- ment to a firm but not registered as its property, make it clear that out of every ten licences in Man- chester at least eight are bound to certain firms of 'brewers for their full supplies. It is urged on behalf of the tied-house system that under it the conduct of public-houses must be improved,because the owner of the house,as owner, becomes directly responsibleto the law. Interest alone—without a care for that character which it is the pride of great business houses to establish— must, it is said, cause the oversight of the brewer to be vigilant and keen. But under the old plan of holding, the publican was in the greater number of cases a man whose savings and capital were to a great extent investend in his house. Such a man by losing his licence would have lost all. The brewer, on the contrary, has no such stake. He pushes responsibility a stage further back, and at once weakens and subdivides it. Viewed in the light of practice, this contention of oversight by the brewer is found to fail entirely. He is careful enough, no doubt, of his monetary stake, but effec- tually shifts his responsibility by the adoption of a system of "transfers on an unlimited scale. By a gradual working of transfers," the brewer from the first began te take the retail trade out of the hands of itsilegitimate holders, and by following up this plan he new contrives that whatever the con- duct of the house its license will remain safe. When I framed, the transfer cluases were clearly intended Ito mean that under a proper ,change of license ownership the power to sell should not at any time I lapse. What they mean under the " tied-house " I system is, that should a " manager" or other holder under the brewer fail in any matter—small returns, declining trade, or breaches of the police code—he can, under "transfer," be quietly and effectually shelvedZand a new servant at once brought in. Un- der the old system transfers were comparatively rare. The license registers of Manchester now show, almost at their first page, licenses which from 1884 up to the lest sessions have undergone eight transfers; others within slightly longer periods have been transfered nine times ; while cases of six and seven transfers within six years are comparatively numerous. None of these transfers occurred with- out reason, or lightly. They were the outcome of numerous police cautions, of much inability to per- suade the public to consume liquor of the character which the brewer chose to supply, of neglected trust If many kinds.'

A. CONFESSION. Mrs. Piercy was hanged in Newgate Jail at eight o'clock on fuesday morning. It was dark until a very short time before the hour of execution. When morningbroke, and the grim outline of Newgate was visible, it was noted that a flagstaff had been erected on the roof of one of the buildings facing the street, and this, with running lines upon it, was grim evidence that the woman was beyond all hope of respite. Few per- sons were about the neighbourhood till about half- past seven o'clock. Between then and a quarter to eight, however, considerable numbers arrived. At a quarter to eight o'clock the bell of St. Sepulchre's began to toll minute strokes. At last there could be seen aim.. every street crowds of men and boys trotting as hard as they could step out to Newgate. Even women and girls joined in the rush, and arrived breathless with- in view of the flagstaff, to which all eyes were upturned in strained watchfulness. Representatives of the press were not admitted to the jail. Only the officials and one or two persons who were unrecognisable as officials, but who entered under official guidance, got within the doors before eight o'clock. Mrs. Piercy rose soon after six 'o'clock. At seven, the Rev. G. H. Duffield, the prison chaplain, went to her cell and remained with her until the time approached for the execution. The unhappy woman ate very little breakfast, but appeared to be quite calm and composed. Sir James Whitehead, high sheriff of the county of London, arrived at the prison a few minutes before eight o'clock, and he at once pro- ceeded to the condemned cell. Shortly afterwards Berry, the executioner, was introduced, and the work of pinioning the culprit was at once performed, not the slightest emotion being exhibited by the unhappy woman. Sir James Whitehead asked her just before proceeding to the scaffold if she had anything to say, as her last moment was then approaching, and she would have no other opportunity of doing so. After a moment's hesitation, she said—" My sentence is a just one, but a good deal of the evidence against me was false." She never uttered another word, but walked firmly to the place of execution, where Berry and his assistant were standing ready to receive her. The rope was quickly adjusted, and, her weight being nine stone, she was given a drop of six feet. Death appeared to be in- stantaneous. On the signal that Berry's task had been accomplished, a loud, exulting cheer went up from the immense crowd stretching away from the entrance to the Old Bailey to the Holborn end of the prison. It was a demonstra- tion in whick the voices of old and young people blended together in a strange chorus of satisfaction that Mrs. Pearcy had paid the penalty of her crime. After hanging for an hour the body was cut down, and Dr. Gilbert, the medical officer of the prison, gave a formal certificate that the culprit was dead. The remains were then placed in a shell to await the coroner's inquest, to be held at noon. - -

- - INQUEST. The inquest upon the body of the dead woman was fixed for noon, the proceedings taking place at the Old Bailey in one of the courts in which the Middlesex Ses- sions are generally heard. Dr. Langham, coroner for the city of London, conducted the inquiry, a jury of 24 persons being sworn. The body having been viewed, Lieutenant-Colonel Milman, the governor of Newgate Prison, the first witness called, produced the warrant of execution of Mary Eleanor Pearcey, alias Wheeler, con- victed of the wilful murder of Phcebe Hogg. He said her age was 24, and she was stated to be married. That was her own statement, but he did not know. She was convicted at the November sessions. In pursuance of the warrant she was executed that morning at Newgate prison, at eight o'clock, in his presence. The body the jury had seen was that of the deceased. The execution, in his opinion, was satisfactory, death being instantaneous. Dr. W. Gilbert, medical officer of New- gate Prison, the next witness, said he was present at the execution, which in every way was satisfactorily carried out. The drop was six feet, and death was due to the spinal cord being divided, the result of hanging. This being all the evidence, the Coroner directed the jury to return a verdict in accordance with the medical testi- mony. This they did at once,and the proceedings ended.

I STRANGE STATEMENT. On Monday, Mr. rearcy, had an interview with her solicitor, Mr. Palmer. She reqested that he should cause an advertisement to be inserted in the Madrid paper; ad- dressed to certain initials, with these words, " Have not betrayed." Surprised at this commission, Mr. Palmer asked whether it had to do with the case. " Never mind," said she. He then asked, "Do you admit the justice of the sentence ? " "No," was the reply, "I do not. I know nothing about the crime." " But, 'it was urged, "even if you did it in a trance, you must have some idea or shadowy recollection of the matter?" " I know nothing about it," she repeated. At the convict's particular and reiterated request,per- mission was given to the man Hogg to visit her between two and four on Monday afternoon, and it was quite evident that she was bent upon seeing him once more. As the time passed on and he did not come she grew somewhat nervous and impatient, and when it was evi- dent that he had resolved to refuse her last request a ter- rible fit of dejection seined her. She lay on her bed with her hands over her face for some time sob- bing, but not speaking. When this was over, and she rose again, her face was calm, her voice had recovered its quiet low tone in speaking,and she resumed her read- ing at the table, without giving any sign of the storm of emotion she had just passed through.
