TRAFFIC DELAYED AND DISORGANISED. OVER 6,000 MEN IDLE. The strike on the Scotch railways practically com- menced on Monday morning, and on the North British and other lines there are more than 6,000 men idle. The firft difficulty was with the signalmen, who left work in a body. Station-masters and other officials who had previously been signalmen were placed in the boxes, and signalled to the best of their knowledge, but there was much delay. Some of the Edinburgh trains were three hours late in leaving Glasgow, and the Hamilton trains two hours behind time. The three railway companies concerned—the North British, the Caledonian, and the Glasgow and South-Western—diminished their ordinary services of passenger trains, striving rather to send out the mail and long-distance trains. A number of local and suburban trains were withdrawn, and there was much grumbling among the business men, particularly those of Glasgow. Not only was there great inconvenience in passenger traffic, but the goods and mineral traffic in some localities of three systems was altogether blocked, seriously checking trade. Pickets were active throughout the day, and there seemed every probability of the strike extending. At a mass meeting of the men in Glas- gow a telegram was read stating that the dispute en the North-Eastern Railway had been settled on most advan- tageous terms, but the workmen were aevertheless pre- pared to stand by their Scotch brethren, and withdraw their labour if necessary. Later news from Edinburgh, Glasgow, and Dundee was to the effect that many additional men had come out, and that there were at least 6,500 on strike. An attempt was made by the pic- kets to stop the Pullman train which runs in connection with the Midland, and at one of the mens' meetings it was stated that the "Flying Scotchman " was detained at Marshall Meadows "for want of signalmen." On Tuesday the strike on the railways was extending. It is stated that there are now more men idle, and that the dispute has already seriously hampered industry, several works and pits having been obliged to cease operations owing to the impossibility of getting goods and coal sent on by rail to customers. In the West Di Scotland luggage trains were almost completely at a standstill, and the outlook on the North British system is becoming serious. The passenger traffic at Queen-st. Station, Glasgow, on Tuesday, for instance, was much disorganised. Additional signalmen had deserted, and there was a scarcity of drivers. Not a train left the station until after eight o'clock in the morning, and only one London express had arrived. The traffic improved very little later, for during the next few hours only , eight trains went out and only three arrived out of a usual service of 54. Some of the suburban and branch ' lines are closed altogether, and many city men had to walk several miles to reach the nearest tramcars. Most of the London trains started considerably behind time. On the Greenock line, a number of signalmen left their cabins, it is asserted without notice, possibly placing , raany passengers in peril. A loop line on the Glasgow and South-Western Railway was closed, and this system is in places almost entirely deserted by signalmen. ' Traffic on the Ayrshire lines is here and there worked without the block system; "in fact there is no signal- ling, and drivers have to make the best of the way over the roads." At their meeting on Tuesday the managers of the various companies decided to continue the struggle. On Christmas Day the position of affairs at Edinburgh and some other centres was worse than on any of the pre- ceding days of the week, the number of strikers having considerably increased. Traffic on the Nurth British Railway was virtually at a standstill, though as regards the Caledonian Railway matters were not quite so bad. The prominent citizens of Edinburgh met on Thursday to consider the situation, and agreed to call a public meet- ing to consider whether the dispute is not one which should be submitted to arbitration. A leading citizen of Glasgow is endeavouring to bring labout a conference be- tween the representatives of the men on strike and the managers of the railways, and it is stated that there is a likelihood of the men agreeing to a joint meeting. The block on the railways converging on Glasgow was on Christmas Day in about the same condition as previously reported. Manufacturers and traders are suffering great inconvenience, and a famine of coal for household as well as for factory use is feared, the prices for both having greatly risen. The Caledonian Railway Company are advertising for engine drivers, firemen, and mineral brakesmen to fill the places of those men who have gone on strike. lin extraordinary incident is reported from Giffnock, on the Caledonian Railway in connection with the strike. A " railway chair" was found securely fastened to the down line. The officials were warned, and it was wrenched off shortly before the train from Kilbride to ellasgow went by.

Two sailors on board the steamship India, lying in the Barry Dock, Liverpool, were suffocated in their berths, on Monday, by the fumes from a pan of coal. third man narrowly escaped. In a Saxon town, on Sunday night, three young men were suffocated by the fumes of charcoal.

MURDER OF A -RITSSIIN LADY.

A recent murder at Moscow having been attributed by the foreign press to Nihilist vengeance, the Russian Government states that the insinuation has no founda- tion in fact. The victim was a lady, and she was mur- dered by her two female servants, who hoped to secure a large sum of money which their mistress was known to keep in the house.

div.head: A. SPORTSMAN SHOT DEAD NEAR WHITBY.
div.p: A. SPORTSMAN SHOT DEAD NEAR WHITBY.

On Tuesday afternoon two brothers, named Brown, who occupy a farm known as Haggit Howe, Whitby, were out shooting wild duck. One of the men was en- gaged in fixing a cap, when the hammer went down, the gun exploded, and the full charge entered the back of his brother, who was removed to an adjacent farmhouse, and died soon afterwards.

div.p: DR. KOCH'S CURE.

TERMS OF STATE PURCHASE. BERLIN, MONDXY.-With regard to the negotiations pending between Dr. Koch and the Government for the State manufacture of the professor's lymph, it is stated this evening that Dr. Koch will receive a sum of 1,000,000 m., and his assistants 500,000 m. In oddition to this the professor will be granted a considerable share of the net profits arising from the sale of the remedy, which is estimated at 1,000,000 m.

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A SHAM I CLERGYMAN. At Barnet on Monday William Gregory Tyler, alias C. W. Tyler, described as a clergyman, was committed for trial, charged with having obtained a situation as curate at Elstree by false iepresentations, and also with having uttered a forged certificate of marriage. A schoolmistress now gave evidence that the prisoner had conducted a form of marriage service between her and himself, and that she sizned a certificate (produced) which was stated by the registrar of marriages for the county of London to be a fraud and a forgery.

div.head: RAILWAY COLLISION AND LOSS OF
div.p: RAILWAY COLLISION AND LOSS OF
LIFE.

The Central News says a serious railway accident oc- curred on Tuesday afternoon, at Broadstone Junction, where the Midland Railway joins the South Western, which resulted in the death of two persons and serious injuries to many others. A Midland train from Birming- ham, due shortly before four o'clock, was entering the station when it was run into with great force by a loco- motive which had passed the signals through some mis- understanding. One carriage was smashed. Two ladies in it were killed and several other passengers were seri- ously injured. Their names are not yet known.

div.p: LOSS OF A LIVERPOOL SHIP BY COLLISION.

- - -- TWENTY-THREE OF THE CREW DROWNED. Lloyd's agent at Pernambuco telegraphed at 3.5 p.m. on Tuesday as follows :—" British ship Talookdar, from Calcutta for London,and the German ship Libussa,from Hamburg for Valparaiso, have been in collision. The former vessel sank. The latter has put in badly dam- aged. Twenty-two of the crew and the captain drowned; remainder landed here. Further particulars will be sent as soon as obtained." The Talookdar was a steel ship of 2,120 tons gross, built at Belfast in 1885, and was owned in Liverpool.

div.head: MESSRS. PETER :WALKER AND SON
div.p: MESSRS. PETER :WALKER AND SON

_ LIMITED. The " Northern Brewers' and Victuallers' Journal" has the following :—Rumour, with a thousand tongues, has been busy for some days past with reference to the sale and purchase of one of the largest brewing basinesses in the provinces. We are in a position to state authoritatively and exclu- sively that the negotiations which for some time past have been ptnding are finally complete, and that the breweries in Soho-st., Liverpool, and at Burton-on-Trent, also upwards of eighty licensed houses and the other business interests of Messrs. Green and Clarkson, have been acquired, absolutely and entirely, by Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, of Warrington and Burton, Limited, at a cost of be tween £300,000 and £400,000. The transfer of the properties, 8,74., takes effect from the first day of the new year. So far as the vendors are concerned this is the largest transaction of the kind ever effected by a private firm, and will be always a notable incident in the general history of the trade.

MR. GLADSTONE ON THE IRISH DIFFICULTY. Mr. Robert Peel, son of the Right Hon. Sirßobert Peel, the accepted Liberal candidate for East Marylebone, has received the following letter from Mr. Gladstone : My Dear Sir,—l view with the heartiest interest your approaching entrance on the political arena, and, as in your father's case, so in your own, it gives me lively pleasure to see the name of Peel associated with the Liberal cause, and especially the cause of Ireland. For the first time since the commencement of her Parliamen- tary struggles under O'Connell, sixty years ago, the Irish party, bent on a constitutional and effective scheme of Home Rule, is looking to Great Britain to pronounce judgment in the contest between it and a minority of its members seceding under Mr. Parnell. The Liberals of Great Britain, who have themselves, since 1886, had to resist and overcome a similar secession, will not doubt on which side they are to recognise the name and true titles of the party and its honourable traditions of resis- tance to wrong. Assuredly, you enter the held at a moment of extreme interest, and one when the cause of wisdom, justice, and freedom has claims upon all who love it enhanced beyond the ordinary standara.—Believe me, very faithfully yours,
W. E. GLADSTONE.

div.p: TRE MURDER IN A LIVERPOOL CAB

PRISONER AND VICTIM. It has been placed beyond doubt that Arthur Pinfold, charged with the murder of a woman in Liverpool, is identified with a grocer's assistant who recently absconded from East Grinstead. The prisoner's brother Charles Phil old, a boot and shoe maker carrying on busi- ness in East Grinstead says that Arthur served in the sth Lancers, and was invalided out of the service suffering with heart disease. He afterwards joined the Sussex Artillery Militia under the name of Peter Bright. He used to complain very much of his head, and the pain was always aggravated by drink. He absconded about a fortnight ago with £lB belonging to his employer. Two of the relatives of the deceased on Sunday called at the Royal Infirmary and identified her as Margaret Stewart, the daughter of an hotel proprietor in Ler- wick. The police are in the possession of evidencc to show that the deceased up till five weeks ago kept a house of ill-fame in a court off Lamhert-st., Liverpool. A Lerwick correspondent telegraphs :—Nothin<> is known here regarding the girl Margaret Stewart': or Cowie, who was murdered in Liverpool last week. So far as acertained, she is certainly not a native of Shet- land, as various reports have represented her to be.

EXPRESS TRIO IN COLLISION. ONE KILLED AND MANY INJURED. An extraordinary railway accident, which in its origin would seem to bear a strong resemblance to the recent disaster near Taunton, occurred on Christmas-eve on the Great Northern line during a heavy fog at Leeds. While a light engine, travelling from Bradford to be stabled for the night at Copley Hill, not far from Leeds Central Station, was standing on the main line, waiting for the signal to cross to the shed road, it was run into by an express train from Liverpool and Manchester due at Leeds at ten minutes east nine o'clock. The force of the collision threw the driver and fireman off the light engine, which then set off down a falling gradient to Leeds station. The runaway locomotive rushed into the statioriat the rate of thirty miles an hour, smashed the buffer stops, and jumped to the platform a complete wreck. One person in the crowd by which the platforms were then occupied. a married woman named White, was struck by the engine and killed. The engine of the express was considerably damaged, and about thirty of its passengers, many of them from Manchester and its neighbourhood, were injured. Official information as to the cause of the accident states that the signalman at Copley Hill forgot the presence of the light engine when he allowed the express to approach.

THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. DECEMBER 27, 1890.

"The Gospel me WE have from ti to time in: of these columns pointed to the enor- Wealth." mous yearly increase of the wealth of the country which is taxing place side by side. with the distressing poverty of the poorest of~tho poor. How to adjust the balance, in some degree,. without revolution, or without doing more harm than good, is a problem which excites, more and. more interest; and it is a healthy sigr that itis now engaging the attention of the bestininds of" the age. There are many hard-headed men who, like Professor HUXLEY, think that nothing but evil can come of attempts to meddle with the social machine; and they do not hesitate to con- demn in advance such schemes,for instanceps that of General BOOTH. They seem to think that im- provement is a matter of evolution of so slow a kind that it is futile to attempt 'to quichin the pace; and they are always ready to condemn the proposals of men whose hearts, as:they would say, run away with their heads. The other da7,Car- dinal MANNING, in a letter on th& labour question, said—" Every man has a right to bread or to work r but Professor HUXLEY this week- expresses-the opinion that the Cardinal's dictum "is a very mis- chievous error." How it becomes a mischievous error be does not explain. POssibly he may think it will do harm by encouraging the idle and dissolute in their improvident habits;. .or ` raw

div.head: it_ok,,Y ab.stradt to- tits use
div.p: it_ok,,Y ab.stradt to- tits use

be that he has some objection in the to the use in this connection of the word "right." It seems to us,, looking at the matter as it effects the people of this counity, that Cardinal MANNING has simply given expres- sion to a truth which may be said to be built into the fabric of the constitution. It is the basis of the,poor-law that no person shall be allowed to die of starvation, and it is furtLer, provided that the person who is relieved shall, if he is able, do a . certain amount of work before he is discharged from the poorhouse. Here we have the right, or title, to, bread, coupled with the injunction to work/ But it is doubtless in a bander sense than this that his Eminence u scs the phrase that "Every man has a right to tread or to work." To begin,with, no man car' be: said to have a choice in..the matter of his p lace of birth. He finds when he arrives in the world, and when he reaches man's estate, that every y ard of English land is claimed by somebody who, with policemen, and, if need be, with soldiers is 3hind him, can say— " Clear out;. don't you t hink of struggling for, existence on my propert: i." If he should help himself to food for which he has not paid, the police will deprive him of his liberty. What then is he to d 0,.? He is no, t allowed to trespass in search of foocl, or to take food without search. He must hire himself out to work for some other, per— son—if he can, Yes, if he can! There's the rub; and it is because he star ids there in his manhood', shut off from the soil, the source of all wealth„ with hunger awl thirst, and a need to be clothed:— and; above all, a willing ness too toil—that Cardinal 111.tuszvirro says---and all except professors will agree with him—" EVi ;ry man has a right to bread or to work."

M.R. ANDREW CARNB ,GIE, the millionaire, recently treated of the uses of wealth and the duties of rich men, n an article in the "Nineteenth Cen- tury." He believes i: n a man who has made money spending it in his lifetime on good objects—. not acquiring a reputation for generosity when his will is read, and whe n he can no longer spend.any- thing., Ms. CARNEME practises what he preaches, as the managers of many Free Libraries well.know. MR:PLADSTONE in :a subsequent paper widened the discussioa by urging the need of an organisation which would perunt man of all. creeds, and, of no cree‘banding themselves together under,a vow to to spend what they could every year in the service of God and their neighbour. Iu the currant issue of the "Nineteenth Century" the tale. is taken up by Cardinal MANNING, Dr. Ames, (Chief .Rabbi) and the Rev. HUGH PRICE Hoonas. The last-named thinks Mr. GLADSTONE is too. amiable, with Mr. @Alonzo= ; for he says—" when I contemplate hint as the representative of a par- ticular class of millionaires, I am forced to say, 'with all pirsonal respect, and ,without holding him in the least responsible for his unfortunate circum- stances, that ho is 'an anti-Christian phenomenon, a social monstrosity„ and a grave political peril." This is a IlaW way of dealing with millionaires, and will be something for them to think about, in conjunction with the text "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon the earth." D. Arame., as a Jew, directs attention to the Old Teitament,and has no diMculty in showing that what Mr. Gunsroxe advocates is strongly enjoined, and is carried out ha the tithe system, which is. still in force amongst his countrymen. The whole of theteath, be says,isto be given to the poor„ not reckoning that even which is devoted to synagog or other ritual uses." Cardinal MAlormo also refers to tithes, and claims that before the Reformation—that is until the six- teenth century—" the poor of England were cared for at t,he doors of the palaces of bishops, :of nobles, of monasteries, and at the thresholds of their pastors and their neighbours." The Church of to-day--not the Cardinal's Church—has the benefit of these ancient tithes, but the poor do not get their share of them as in the olden time. Hence the need for such practice of personal charity as that proposed by Mr, GLADSTONE. ST. JOHN'S BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN. The members of this Society gave an entertainment on Tuesdaf evening to a good audience. A capital pro- gramme was gone through. Mr. James Kirkham pre- sided. ST. JOHN'S BIBLE CLASS AND LITERARY GUILD, RUNCORN. At a meeting on Monday evening, Mr. C. Cowley, the secretary, read an able paper on "Oliver Cromwell." The Rev. J. Pulford Williams presided.

- - - - • TUE FROST AT WIDNES. Frost and snow prevailed in this neighbourhood for a week, up to Wednesday last, and threw large numbers of men out of employment. The supply of gas in con- sequence of the freezing of the meters, was Interfered with,and tradesmen suffered considerable inconvenience. SOU-WF.STER HOOF PLATES.—J. S. Garland, Builders' Iron- monger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt.

- - - WIDNES POLICE COURT. Before Mr. H. W. Deacon at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, Peter Fletcher, Marshall Cross, Bt. Helens, was charged with havingbegged alms frem door to door at Appleton by means of a letter. He was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.—John Johnstone, no settled resi- dence, was charged with stealing from the pawnshop of Mrs. unison in Waterloo-road, on Tuesday night eleven pairs of trousers, and two leather straps, worth £1 us. 9d. The prisoner was remanded for a week. DUTTON PENNY BANK. In July, 1887, the master of the above schools (Mr. Sydney B. Stokes), as a. means of encouraging thrift amongst the children, started a Penny Bank in connection with the Post Office. The miwernent is one which reflects the highest credit on Mr. Stokes. The Venture has been a great success, for at the preseat time there are 87 de- positors, with a total sum of over £lOO standing to their credit in the Post Office Eavings Bank, the Government giving 4 per cent. interest for the use of the money. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W DUTTON'S Sankey-at.. Warrington.—Advt.

ST: MICHAEL'S PARISH CHURCH, DITTON. A children's cantata, entitled" A Merry Party," was given in St. Michael's Parish Schools, Hough Green, on Monday evening to a very good audience. The Vicar, Rev. C. W. Wooll, presided, and the chief characters were taken by the following :--Misses E. M. Barker, Nellie Davies, Fanny Hosker, Florrie Lyons, A. Hosker, Maggie Miller, A. Q. Burnley. Masters John Ambridge, It. II irrison, John Swain, John Hudson, James Cook,and Tom Foruear. Miss M. M. Barker acted as accompanist.

DU'TTON BOARD SCHOOL. The annual prize distribution to the scholars attending the Board School took place on Wednesday, when Mr: John Smith (chairman of the Board) attended, and after giving some good advice, regarding punctuality, regular attendance, &c., presented the prizes,' con- sisting of valuable books, to 52 of the scholars for diligence and attendance. The master, having, on , behalf of the children, thanked Mr. Smith for his kind- ' ness, afterwards dismissed them for the Christmas vaca- tion. The school will be re-opened on Monday, the sth January, 1890. HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN. With the object of clearing off a debt on the day schools and renovating the church; it is proposed to hold a bazaar early in the New Year and a Committee has been formed with Mr. J. Meadowcroft as treasurer, and Mr. T. H. Annett as secretary to make the necessary arrange- ments. The lady members of the congregation have commenced work for a bazaar, and as there has not been a bazaar in connection with Holy Trinity for 18 years, ' confident hopes are entertained that generous support will be accorded and that the amount needed—about £3oo—will be raised. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-3. AW. Dirrrox's Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. DEATH OF A RUNCORN TRADESMAN. We regret to announce the death of Mr. Joseph Richardson, butcher, of Devonshire Square, which oc- curred on Tuesday night from acute bronchitis. Mr. Richardson who had attained the age of 60 years, had lived in Runcorn the greater portion of his life, and had for a period of over 20 years, kept the shop in which he died. Some years ago he had amassed a considerable fortune by his business, but trade losses and the posses- sion of a too generous disposition had reduced it to very limited proportions at thatime of his demise.. He was a friend indeed to many,a friend and acquaintance in need, and for several years he had been a most liberal sub- scriber to the salvation Army, whose work amongst the IYI4 sseS had his approval. , • • , AN UNGRATEFUL THIEF AT RUNCORN. George Torigallas Sussex Bandy, a Ship Canal 'labourer, went to the house of William Davies, 41 King- street, Runcorn, on Friday, and agile had Itidgect for a short time previously, Mrs. Davies allowed him to rest on the sofa. She went out to transact some business, and on returning half an hour later she met the prisoner coming away from the house. She observed that her son's moneybox, which was on the mantelpiece, had been tampered with, and found that the six shillings which it had contained had been taken. Information was given at the police station, and Detective Officer Woodrow discovered the prisoner hiding behind a cart in Nelson-street. The prisoner had 4s. 2d. upon him, and a knife which appeared to have been used in forc- ing open the bo-t. He denied the theft, but he was brought before Mr. Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst on Wednesday, and sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. PRESENTATION TO THE SHIP CANAL MISSIONARY AT

Rl;Nconn. During the course of a service of song "Her Benny " at the Ship Canal Mksion Room, Runcorn, on Monday evening, a presentation was made to Mr. John Watson, who for the oast three years has worked earnestly and successfully amotigst the navvies of the Runcorn Section of the Canal. The present consisted of a purse of gold and a handsome black marble timepiece, which bore the inscription "Presented to Mr. John Watson as a token of esteem by the workmen and friends on his leaving the Canal Mission, Runcorn, Dec. 1890." Mr. J. Weston, the agent for the section, presided, and in hand- ing the testimonial to Mr. Watson, remarked that he had gained the goodwill and esteem of all sections of work- men on the canal, as well as of the officials. He trusted Mr. Watson's future would be happy and suc- cessful.—ln acknowledgina the gift Mr. Watson said he had endeavoured to do his duty, but had,he knew,failed very often.' He was pleased te:wever that his services had been appreciated,ind he should look upon the timepiece in years to come as a token of the esteem of his friends in Runcorn.—The service of song was then proceeded with. Mrs. Joynson was the organist, Mr. Valentine Wright the conductor, and Mrs. Foster the reader. The proceeds are to be devoted to a Children's Christmas Tree. • SIR A. B. WALKER. On Tuesday afternoon, at the Walker Art Gal- lery, Liverpool, a presentation was made to Sir A. B. Walker of his portrait, which has been painted by Mr. W. 0. Orchardson, R.A. The portrait has been painted on the commission of a number of gentlemen who desired to commemorate the services which Sir A. B. Walker. recently rendered as High Sheriff of Lancashire. MASONIC INSTALLATION AT _ASHTON.

The members of the Faith Lodge No. 484 Ashton, of Freemasons, celebrated the festival of St. John at the Lodge Rooms, Gerard Arms'llotel, Asht on on Tuesday evening. An installation ceremony was also carried through, Bro. F. Harwood, P.M., instal- ling Bro. V. Aspinall aa the W.M. for the ensuing year. After the installation, the W.M. proceeded to ,invest his officers fa the ensuing year. After the ceremony, the brethren celebrated the festival of St. John, at the Gerard Arms, about 40 sitting down to an excellent repast. HOT WATER HEATING.—Garland sends estimates free. Warrington.—Advt. , A RUNCORN CAPTAIN IN SOI7TH Arlt/CA. A few days ago Mr. H. Rigby, of Greenway-rd., Runcorn, captain of the Castle Royal Mail Steamer,. Pembroke Castle, brought his fine ship into the port of London• after a very successful passage to and from South Africa. On the outward journey amongst the passengers was Sir Somers Vine, assis- tant secretary to the Imperial Institute who em- barked at Natal, and haying important and urgent business to transact at Mauritius, Captain Rigby made the quickest passage he could to that place. On arrival there his knowledge of the locality and of the people enabled him to give Sir Somers some highly useful information, and to introduce him to a number of gentlemen who could be of the greatest assistance to the Imperial Institute. On landing in London Captain Rigby was placed in possession i of a letter which had been addressed n care of Messrs. Donald, Currie and Co., the owners of the Pembroke Castle; thanking him in the name of the Prince of Wales for the great service he ren- dered te the Assistant Secretary of the Imperial Institute.

THE INSTITUTE OF JOURNALISTS; " The quarterly. meeting of the Liverpool District of the Chartered Institute of Journalists was held; on Saturday, at Southport, When Mr. W. G. Flynt, the retiring'chairman presided over an attendance of thirty members, the Liverpool; Wigan, Chester, Warrington, Southport, and other sub-districts being represented. Members from a distance were received in the boardroom Of Messrs. Robert Johnson and Co. Limited, by Mr. J. A. Robinson J.P., chairman of the directors, and after a tour of the commodious new" Viaiter " printing works, which were much admired, the directors entertained the delegates to luncheon at the Prince of Wales Hotel, Mr. Robinson being there supported by his co-directors, Mr. Chas. Scansbrick, J.P., and Mr. G H. Thorniley, J.P., and Mr. R. H. Johnson, secretary and manager, who each extended a welcome to the members of the Institute. A short toast list was gone through, and then the delegates repaired to the Town Hall, where the Mayor (Mr. A. Pilling), received them in his parlour, and in company with the Mayoress remained during: the business meeting, which occupied over two hours. Some correspondence with the central office having been considered, it was resolved that the district maintain the ".home rule principle" to the extent of having absolute control over a third of its subscriptions. The honorary district secretary and treasurer (Mr. J. Mason) signified his intention, owing to pressure of other duties, to retire at the annual meeting in February when it was resolved to ask the District Committee to receive nominations for the treasurership, and to instruct Mr. Mason to seek a co-secretary for next year. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman and directors of the " Visiter " Company for their hospitality. The Mayor and 3laynnisB.entertained the delegates to -tea. "OK. YES!" ESCAPE OF A LIONESS.AT WIDNES : EXCITING SCENE; On Monday, a lioness belonging to Wombwell's Menagerie escaped out of a van on the London and North-Western goods line at Widnes. Wombwell's Menagene visited the town on Friday, and on leav- ing the following rahruing they sent one of their " live " vans to the goods yard as empty. to be for- warded to Bolton. This van.it has since been found out, contained a box with a lioness in it. By some means the animal managed to get out of the box, and escaped from the van by a glass window, which was found to be broken, The lioness was seen by the rai I wav men at Dit ton Station walking along the line. They went to a signal-box close at hand, and sent wad to Halebank for some one to ineQt it there with a gun. Subsequently shortly before eight o'clock on Monday morning, ft scene of much excite- ment.was witnessed at Halebank Railway station, in consequence of the appearance of the lioness on the platform. A porter while walking along tile platform suddenly found himself within a few paces of the animal, which he had not before observed in the dim morning light. As the lioness showed a bold front the porter naturally turned and made off as fast as he could from such dangerous company. While running he raised such an alarm as caused a general stampede from the station premises, the doors of which were locked by Mr. Needs, the , station master,with the double object of preventing 1 the lioness from escaping or any one from entering. , Mr. Needs then sent for Mr.Nitylor and Mr. Mercer a couple of neighbouring farmers, who arrived shortly afterwards with their guns, and one of them lodged a shot in the animal's neck. This so 'much disabled it as to allow a blow with a heavy hammer being given on the head with such effect as to terminate its existence. The lioness did not attempt to attack any one during its walk although it passed several men. MII.."'LLAS RE-COYERED at the shortest notice.—J. DUTTONs Sankey-st., Warrlngton.-4.4e.t.

The following comment on tllb health of War- rington appears in the December issue of the "Sanitary Record" :—" Warrington (population, 49,000). The chief sanitary interest in Mr.. Gorn- all's report for 1889 is to be found in a summary of the fever cases of the year, and an account of the conditions surrounding the dwellings. In a few brief re-narks Mr. Gornall asks that attention may be directed to the serious evils arising from "the unhealthy areas" and "unsanitary dwellings" which still exist in the borough. A description of these is to be found in a small supplementary re- port narrating the general conditions of two of the worst wards. This evidence of the need of improve- ment is further emphasised by the statistics of zymotic mortality for the past ten years, the so called filth diseases annually contributing steadily their quota. The year 1889 was a favourable one, and the death-rate showed the large increase of 2-6 upon the rate of 1888. This was mainly due to an epidemic of measles. As in so many other districts, diphtheria and croup appear to be gaining in virulence." UMBREISAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-7. & W. DurrOX'S sankey-at, Warrington.—Advi.

BY "AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDEN'T_ :"

- - During the existence of the Runoorn Y.M.C.A., one of the events of the year was the Aged Persons Treat, which brought together between 500 and 600 of the oldest inhabitants of the place, and I am glad that Mr. Taylor, chairman of the Commis- sioners, acted upon a requisition presented to him, and called a meeting to arrange a revival of the treat. The meeting was of very small proportions but amply sufficient to set the machinery in motion, and this is to be done at once. Mr. Simpson objected to the title of the treat, which he argued included the word" poor," in the past, but a reference to the published reports would show that this is an error. It was in no wise regarded as relieving the necessit- ous, but rather to bring the old people of the place together in an endeavour as Mr. Coventry aptly put it" to throw a ray of sunshine and a gleam of happinessinto their hearts," There are always those who are ready to abuse generosity of any description, but if the many who are benefited, the promoters ot the treat may 'disregard the few. Mr. Brunner, M.P., on Saturday last distributed the prizes to the successful students at the north- wich Science and Art School, and in the course of his speech he made several complimentary refer- ences to the condition of education in Runcorn. It is gratifying that Mr. Brunner has so high an opin- ion of us in that respect, but I doubt whether our public authorities are entitled to the encomiums passed upon them. As regards elementary educa- tion the townspeople have no reason to grumble, but as regards opportunities for continuing educa- tion after leaving school, Runcorn is very far indeed behind many Lancashire towns. The School Board have this winter conferred a boon upon the youth of the town by establishing even- ing classes, which are well attended, and in allowing Mr. Cook to establish an art class, but in fact and according to the report of the Technical Instruction Committee much remains to be done. The Lancashire County Council have determined to devote their funds from the Local Taxation Act to the advancement of technical instruction by a system of grants on the system of payment by result. Should the Cheshire C. C. adopt a similar method it is interesting to sur- mise what would be the reply to Runcorn's appeal for a building grant, and should such a grant be declined what action our local rulers wouldtake in regard to the subject. We can only say watch and wait. I have before pointed out what Co-operative Societies in other towns accomplish in the cause of education, while in Runcorn the shareholders do nothing besides purchase their goods and pocket the" divi." Might I suggest that they out of the fulness of their coppers make a grant towards the establishment of a technical school, when a prac- tical scheme is adopted, and thus confer a blessing upon their children, and the children of the towns- people generally? Mr. H. A. R. Davenport,sub-agent of the Runcorn section of the Ship Canal Works, is spending his Christmas holidays at his home in Rent. Before he returns he will have joined the "noble army of benedicts," and the workmen have displayed their good wishes for his future happiness and that of his bride by presenting him with a handsome silver tea and coffee service.

div.head: PROPOSED REVIVAL OF THE AGED PERSONS' TREAT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: PROPOSED REVIVAL OF THE AGED PERSONS' TREAT AT RUNCORN.

One of the most successful and widely appreci- ated schemes of the now defunct Y.M.C.A., was the annual provision of an aged persons' treat,to which all 60 years of age and over were invited,preference, of course, being given to those who were not in prosperous circumstances. The Committee in the exercise of their discretion did not press unduly the age limit, and the gathering became a most pleasant and interesting reunion. With a view of resuming this annual entertainment of the aged people, a meeting called by Mr. S. Taylor, the chair- man of the Board of Commissioners, was held in the' Town Hall on Monday night when, besides Mr. Taylor, who occupied the chair, there were present the Revs. H. Burson (Wesleyan), J. Holden (Church), , and A. Finch (Primitive Methodist) • Messrs. .1. Simpson. W. Shaw (Seamen's Missionary), J. Howitt, F. J. Norman, S. Coventry, J. W. Wooland, J. D.. Jones, and Captain Le Couteur.—The Chairman explained that he had called the meeting in response to a signed requisition, andTe- marked that if the aged peoples' treat could be revived, it would give a great amount of pleasure and happiness to them.' (Hear, hear.) He was sure that the move- ment would have the sympathy and support of everyone in Runcorn. (year, hear.)—Mr. F. .J. Norman moved "That it is desirable to revive the Runcorn Aged Peoples' Treat and that a committee be appointed to manage the same." He said those who had had to do with the treat when given by the now defunct Y.M.C.A., would re- member that it was highly successful, and if it could be worked on the same lines and kept from denomina- tionalism, it would be quite as much a success this year as in years past. (Beer, hear.)—Mr. W. Shaw seconded the motion, and agreed that the movement should in no wise be tainted with denominationalism. He was glad there was a prospect of the treat being revived and he should be pleased to do his share cowards making it a success.—Mr. J. Simpson said the treat when man- aged by the Y.M.C.A., was understood to be a treat to the aged poor people, and great dissatisfaction was caused by the fact that many persons who could not be considered poor received tickets and were admitted. Neither be nor Captain Le Uouteur wanted a subscrip- tion raising to give themselves a treat, and yet if the treat was for aged persons' they should be included in that category. If they raised a fund for an aged peoples treat where were they going to draw the line? All the aged persons in the town would have a right of admis- sion to the treat, but if they called it an aged poor peoples' treat they would be able to discriminate between those who were really called poor and those who were not.—Mr. Flowitt acknowledged the difficulty of drawing the line as to who were poor and who were not; but he should never ask Mr. Simpson to sit down at the table, , knowing his position. There were many people on the verge of poverty who did not call theinselvel poor, and whe would be thankful for a good meal, but he (Mr. Howitt) did not think they should be tainted with the name of paupers. (Hear, he..r.) He went in far giving the treat to the old people, believing that his friend Mr. Simpson would do likewise out of the fulness of his soul and the fulness of his pocket.—The Rev. S. Holden surmised that in the past the teat been called "The old people's treat," but , the Committee were not infallible, and some undeserving 1 persons might have .got tickets. if they wanted to do a kind thing let them do it in the kindest- way possible. The Committee would have a good idea of the applicants and would discriminate between who were really poor and who were comparatively well off. (Hear, hear.)— The Rev. H. Burson said Ile did not know whether that meeting was sufficiently representative to take notice of the matter. If the present very sharp weather con- tinned, to give one meal would be totally inadequate, as there would be a great number of families on the verge of absolute want. What would be the good of giving one meal in the middle of January? It was their duty to begin at once and see what they could do for the people out of work and who would soon want bread and erin.g.—Mr. Howitt said titis Scheme was only a prelude to ' What might follow, If it was found neceSsary, he was t Willing to'guarantte a a mouth toWardS a soup kitchen. —The Rev. H. J. Holden said there were many grateful hearts in Runcorn who felt for the poor, and who would subscribe towards a soup kitchen if it were necessary.— The Rev. H. Burson thought with regara to the treat under consideration, that it should be understood the persons who got tickets shqhld be needy, and that the title of the treat should remain as it was, for if the word " poor " were added, it would humiliate some people. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Simpson said when they provided a treat, they said it was intended for the ' ioor, and be ~ •, I i could not understand -' l i - ivny it shoutu of go forth to the public that it ; t..i. i. -was iittended for the poor. fie Ctlected iEn it being dalldi the aged people's treat, and he objected to being included in that funcL—Captain Le Couteur said there were many aged people who would rather purchase tickets at I.S. or I.s. 6d. than miss the treat.—Mr. Norman said those Who were stated to be comparatively opalent persons, who had been present at a previous treat laZ6 paid is. ed. for their tickets; let it be understood that the same system would again be adopted.—Mr. Simpson said ho had heard of men who were in regular work and had been for years, being present and he believed that they did not pay for their tea.—Mr. Coven- try said the treat was never stated to be for the aged poor. It was an aged peoples' re-union and if they could throw a ray of sunshine and a gleam of happiness across their path when everyone was enjoying themselves they would do a great deal of good for the aged people of the town. (Hear, hear.) In the first every inquiry had been made beforehand, and as it was discovered afterward's that there were cases where some aged people had been forgotten tickets were left with certain tradesmen, and a few people got two tickets by mistake, but this had since been guarded against.—The Chairman remarked that there was a certain amount of imposition,and when they intended to do good they, m ust make some allowance. (Hear, hear.) He always felt grateful when he had done good if he only relieved 70 per cent, of persons who were deserving, because he always looked upon charity in the light of trying to do good,and he. closed his eyes to slight cases of imposition. (Hear, hoar.) There were many people who would resent being termed. poor, and he ad- mired their spirit because he was convinced the really poor wanted looking up. If they wanted to do good they 1 must take a broad view of the question, and if a few got into the treat for whom it was never intended, never mind, it would do their hearts good. (Hear, hear.) They were only quibbling over a word, and he thought the term" Aged people's treat " would be less objeetionable than the term" Aged poor people's treat."—The motion on being put to the meeting was carried, Mr. Simpson only voting against.—A Committee of Management was then appointed, with Mr. Taylor as chairman, Mr. J. D. Jones, Mr.W. B. Frith and Mr. H. Wright secretaries and Mr. J. B. Holland treasurer. It was understood the treat would be given in January. ,

div.p: WIDNES.

Theleatiyal of the nativity was celebrated in the, usual quiet fashion in these towns. It is essentially a time of ieasing and the tradesmen made a • great I display of their goods to attract purchasers, of whom there was no lack, as trade has been. getter- ally,good during the past twelve months. The frost 'of the past ten days has unfortunately thrown'many outdoor workmen out of employment, and they have lost wages they ,could ill spare; but there aro no cases of severe distress in the nei,g,hbohrliood. The thaw of the previous two .days had 'given place. to a keen frost, and people wk.ie able to rejoice in an "old-fashioned Cliristartas." The skaters made the most of their opportunity, and the Big • Pool, which was .covered with thick ice was crowded with hundreds of people. The streets generally had . a deserted appearance, family parties being the order of the day, but those who wished to travel to visit friends had the dis- comfort of walking to Widnes, as the Runcoru railway station was closed. In the morning services wc re conducted at the churches of the Establish- ment, which were appropriately decorated for the occasion. A service was also held at St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, where the Rev. 11. Bur- son preached an appropriate sermon, and service was also held at Victoria-road Wesleyan. Chapel, Widnss. At the several Catholic churches in the neighbourhood High Mass was celebrated. None have, felt the severe weather more than the canal boatmen, and Mr. W. Shaw, the missionary of the Mersey Missions, having obtained help from a number of friends interested in their wel- fare, provided a capital dinner for about 100 persons at the Mission Room, Bottom Locks. In connection with Newtown Mission School, soup was provided to about 80 poor people. Mrs. W. Whittaker, of Higher Runcorn, had kindly under- taken the task of making the soup and assisted by workers from the school, it was distributed by her at noon on Christmas Day, together with a quantity of bread. Each person was given according to the family they possessed and it was cordially wel- comed in every case.

The Moral Nov Liberals alone, but all who of love truth and virtue have reason Kilkenny. to rejoice at the result of the elec- tion for North Kilkenny. The contest has not been a contest between candidates; it has been a struggle between a cause and a man ; between a cause on, the eve of triumph, and a man who, ruined in reputation, seeks to ruin the party which no longer recognises him as its leader. Mr. PAR- NELL has been cast outby the constitutional repre- sentatives of Ireland, and he is now cast out by the electors of Kilkenny. A majority against him of 1,162 is not merely a repulse : it is a crushing defeat. He still breathes threatenings and slaughter; but his fire and tow are not likely now to burn up anybody but himself. It is mere raving to talk about a conspiracy against him. A man who stands cOnvicted in the Divorce Court, who betrays his country by betraying the confi- dence of statesmen, and who seeks to brazen it out by giving the lie to all who have implicitly trusted him, requires no conspiracy to account for his fall, except the conspiracy within himself and against himself, which has caused him to fall, "like Lucifer, never to hope again." He has mistaken the Irish as he has mistaken the English people in thinking his genius for leadership was such that he would be tolerated as "a char- tered libertine" who would be permitted, as he pleased, to break all moral laws. Not so ; he ought to have thought of Tennyson's lines— What! Lave we fought for freedom from our prime, At last to dodge and palter with a public crime? , His shamelessness in speaking, after the election, of bearing a "banner unstained unsullied" is indi- cative of such-utter demoralisation as to suggest that he is on the borderland of lunacy. But mad or bad, he can DO longer be regarded as the leader of the Irish people. He has appealed to. Cresar, and Cresar has declared against him. If he is strong enough to continue the campaign which he threatens, he will have to rely upon the rowdy element in Ireland—the element that he has hitherto ignored and despised. He has appealed to the hillside men, but they have not responded. They do not trust him; they have never trusted him; and how can they trust him now when per- aonal.ambition has caused him to trample patrio- tism under foot? Nor is it likely that he will be more successful in his bid for the votes of the labouring classes. They must know that he has not done a stroke of work for them, but that he has, on thc contrary, given the cold shoulder to men like Mr. 31104z1. DAVITT who were disposed to push their claims to the front. Where was he when the Labourers' Dwellings Bill vf as before Parliament ? Whena-has he- bectrolia hundrect occasions when ho ought to have been in the thick I of the fight. 111, it may be granted, sometimes; but it is now known that at other times he was in hiding as Fox, or CirarsELL, or STEWART, or Pitmen., in order that he might the more suc- cessfully pursue his guilty intrigue with another man's wife. Ireland is beginning to realise all this as is4shown by the polling at Kilkenny. Mr. Pensmar; got the start, and, at the beginning, he more than held his own; but, as the truth about him became known, it was seen that he had put himself beyond the pale—that from being a help he had become a hindrance to the cause of Home Rule. That is how the matter stands to-day. Moral force is stronger than personal force. As the evil man becomes weak, the good cause will again I become strong.

It was feared that the indifferent health from which the Speaker has suffered, together with the loss of his wife, would lead to his retirement ;but it is now stated that he will resume his duties upon the opening of Parliament. The office carries with it a salary of £5,000 a year' with,in the usual order of things, a peerage on retirement. Mr. Peel has made, on the whole, a good Speaker ; he is in, every way a better man than Sir Robert, his eldest brother, who cannot, be said. to have made the most of his great name and exceptionaloppoirtuni- tics.

The records vary somewhat as to the lowest tem- perature during the recent frost. The record at Winwick for last night week was as follows : " Maximum, 28 deg. ; minimum, 3 deg.; shade at nine o'clock, 10 deg. ; exposure at nine o'clock, 6 deg." There has since, according to one autho- rity, been a still lower register. Mr. W. F. Thomas, Manor House, Southall, writing on Wednesday to the "Daily NewaT aays :—"As an instance of very low temperature, it may interest your readers to know that here in Middlesex, at six o'clock on Tuesday night, oue of Negretti's instruments on the snow registered one degree below zero."

The divinity which is said to hedge a King is not supposed to extend to the King's son, or the British Government would not have suggested that a tiger-hunt should not form part of the programme during the visit of the Czarewitch to India. Tiger- hunting is exciting sport, but it becomes too ex- citing when, as sometimes happens, instead of the man hunting the tiger, the tiger takes to hunting 1 the man. The Czar has been appealed to, and he has left it to the Grand Duke in charge to hunt or not hunt as he may deem best; so the chances are that the young blood will be allowed to see sport. •

"A lion in the path " is a phrase which is very often used, but it is a mere metaphor of course in this country—except about once m a generation. The exception occurred on Monday morning when the porter at Hale Bank Station found a lion or lioness walking towards him. He ran, and fortun- ately the rual beast was too indifferent at the moment to run after him. A farmer's gun shortly afterwards put an end to the creature's life. It seems the lioness had escaped from a railway van at Widnes, and had taken an early walk in the direction of Liverpool.

- -- -- As will be seen from the report in another column, a flint-glass blower of St. Helens perished through exposure to the weather on Friday night. He had taken too much liquor with a number of fellow-vborkmen, and was making his way home when he wandered into a field, and wandered round it three or four times before falling down into the sloep that knew no waking It would seem that, in his final delirium' he had partially undressed, as if going to bed. The post-mortem revealed a singular record of the terrible severity of the weather, for it was found that the poor fellow's blood ,was frozen, and that there was ice in the stomach and heart.

There —7a well-grounded and growing opinion that the se of gas in lighting rooms has a vitiat- ing eife6t upon the atmosphere. The point was dw,eit upon by Professor Lewes in a lecture which Joe delivered before the Society of Arts, in London, on Monday. The mischief is increased by the use of globes, which intercept the light, and necessit- ate the use of a larger number of burners than would btherwise be required. In nine cases out of ten, where four lights are used, two would give quite as much illumination if the globes were re- moved. Itwould be out of place to say anything about reducing gas bills, for people who use fancy globes do not, of course, study economy. The Bishop of Salisbury believes in consecra- tion; he will have 'nothing to do with dedication, and has refused to take part in dedicating the new cemetery of Wilton. He holds that without consecration the cemetery would not be dis- tinguished from other common ground." It would be interesting to ascertain if it would be possible to distinguish the differance from " com- mon ground" alter the application, say, of "a forty-parson power" of consecration. But why should Dr. Wordsworth trouble ? "After life's fitful fever," the dead sleep well, be the earth in which they lie dedicated, or consecrated, or even "common ground."

Tennyson, by-the-bye used both words as an artist in the Dedication of his "Idylls of the King " to" Albert the Good." The lines run ; These tohis memory since he held them dear, --Perchance as finding there unconsciously Some image of himself,—l dedicate, • I dedicate, I consecrate, with tears— These Idylls. This is a short- service, although undoubtedly a noble one; and if the Bishop of Salisbury could dedicate and consecrate a new cemetery with as little fuss and formality, and apart from legal obli- gations, he would render a real service to tho in- habitants of Wilton.

The sad loss of life near Liverpool from the ex- plosion of a kitchen boiler, on Sunday, has brought terror to many a household, particularly as it has been followed by other explosions, though not fatal ones. We give in another column some prac- tical advice as to what should be done. There are, howevar,so many systems of hot water supply, that what holds good of one case may not apply to another. It is the duty of the head of the family to know what system is in use in his own house; and frequently test the taps, &c., during frost. Whenever ,it happens that water cannot be drawn from the kitchen boiler, it is a safe rule to put out the fire until some competent person can say that it is safe to re-light it.

Widnes Cricket 'Club, a concert was given in Alexandra Theatre, on Saturday night. A capital miscellaneous programme was carried out by Messrs. J. Morrison, H. W.- Deacon, J. W. White, W. Efulth,LAL Lea' F. W. Wareing, A. Barry, and the •'Widnes Mohawk Minstrels. The entertainment concluded with a performance of the farce "Area Belle," by the members of the Widnes Dramatic Society. Satnuel Henry Pink, Vicar of Chapel-en-le-; Frith, Derbyshire, died on Wednesday, after a few days' illness. In the early part of his career Mr. Pink was stationed at Runcorn as- a Wesleyan minister, when he iermed the aequ'aintitkee of Miss F. Hazlehurst, daughter of Mr. Charles Hazlehurbt, of the Grange, who subse- quently became his wife. On leaving Runcorn, he joined the Established Church, and was appointed curate-in-charge of the church of Chariel-en-le-Frith.and five years ago he was elected vicar by the voted of the parishioners. On Wednesday, the 17th inst., Mr. Thomas Beecham the well-known pill manufacturer of St. Helens, received a letter asking for a contribution in aid of a free break- fast for poor people at Widnes. The missive was signed " Douglas " and Mr. Beecham was directed to address his reply to "The Rev. J. H. Douglas, Widnes." Sus- pecting that everything was not as it seemed, Mr. Beecham, instead of forwarding a donation, communi- cated with the Widnes police, and a youth named John Jas. Bennett was arrested on a charge of attempting to obtain charitable contributions by false pretences. He was brought before Mr. Gossage on Saturday morning, and pleaded guilty. His advocate, Mr. J W: Knowles: in mitigation of punishment pleaded that the prisoner was out of employment, and this was his first offence. A fine of 20s. was imposed, or, in default a month's imprisonment. STABBING AFFRAY AT WIDNES ON CHRISTMAS EVE. Yesterday at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. H. Wade Deacon,Edward Hynan, labourer, Nelson-st. , was charged with having wounded Michael John Keegan, labourer, of 46, Wellington-St., with intent to do him some bodily harm. The men were drinking together in several public. houses from 5 p.m. to 11 p.m. on Christmas Eve. After- wards they went to the home of the prisoner's father, where an altercation took place in an adjoining entry. The prisoner struck Keegan with his fist and the latter returned the blow, whereupon the prisoner went into his own house and returning stabbed Keegan twice with a knife, inflicting a serious wound on the right arm and left shoulder. Keegan attempted to run away but fell, and several persons present took him to Dr. Hutchinson's surgery. ,As the injured man would not be able to ap- pear for a week, the prisoner was remanded for a week on the application of Superintendent Noblett. div.head: FROST AT RUSCORN.
div.p: THE FROST AT RUSCORN.
RIDTDRANCE TO NAVIGATION.

The frost and snow of the latter end of last week and the beginning of the present week has been a source of great inconvenience to the people of Run- corn, and a serious disturbance to trade. Outdoor employment was to a large extent out of the ques- tion,. and masons and hricksetters and other artisans have been in idleness for a week. To the poor the problem of existence is always a difficult one to solve, and the severe cold has not made it any easier. There is considerable scope for the display of generosity by the charitable, and gifts of coal, which has risen to the high figure of £1 a ton would be welcome in many quarters. One very serious effect of the severe weather has been the stoppage of the Bridgewater eanal, by means lof which enormous quantities of goods are conveyed be- tween Manchester and Liverpool. On Sunday the canal was completely icebound, but a strong tug boat and the ice boat succeeded in forcing a passage, through which a small percentage of the traffic was conducted. On Monday the surface was again covered with a thick coating of ice, and the efforts made to break it up suffi- ciently to enable the traffic to be conducted were not successful. In fact the tug boat drawing the ice boat often recoiled seberal feet on colliding with the be. Traffic on Monday was therefore at a standstill. A thaw set in onTuesday,but the impediment to navigation continued Traffic was not resumed until Wednesday morning when the tug boats were depatched to Manchester, but draw- ing not mare than one third of the usual number of fiats. We believe that so severe a frost on this canal has not been experienced since 184.8. Formerly the Runcorn and Latchford Canal, was a great aid to the Company in con ducting their business, as it was a stream of flowing water and available for navigation a month after the other canal was closed, but this waterway is now extinct and the trade has to be conducted from Warrington on the Mersey. On Monday the steam Brackley met with so many and so heavy minature icebergs that she did not arrive at Runcorn with her train flats till after high water and too late to proceed to Liverpool. In fact the Mersey was filled with floating ice,which, although plea- sant to view, was a great hindrance to the trade of the port. Operations in the construction of the Ship Canal were stopped through the frost, and work will not be re- umed until after the Xmas holidays.

div.head: JAPANESE EXHIBITS AT THE MUSEUM.
div.p: JAPANESE EXHIBITS AT THE MUSEUM.

As we mentioned very briefly last week, there are at present on view, in the Warrington Museum, a most interesting coltection of Japanese paintings, and specimens to illustrate the uses of the bamboo , in Japan. These exhibits will be at the Museum ; for some weeks to come, and we should certainly , advise all our readers' who can make it convenient to pay a visit to that institution before the pictures and specimens are withdrawn and sent back to their owner, Mr. C. 110 l in es, of Bexley Heath, Kent, who has been so kind as to place them for the time being at the disposal of t.,e Curator, Mr. Madeley. ' All the visitors to the Museum, who desire them, are ' freely supplied with catalogues, which contain a ' list and descriptive account of the exhibits. In explanation of the manner in which many of the ! pictures are hung, we are told that paintings in Japan ' are generally mounted upon rollers as maps are in ! Europe, and in this form are called hanging pictures. In the guest room of a Japanese house there is always in one of the side walls a recess with raised floor, like a museum ease with the glass front removed. In this re- cess, and nowhere else, a single picture is hung. If the owner possesses more than one picture they will 1, be exhibited in turn, being stowed away meanwhile in a : fire-proof building in the garden, along with the other treasures of the family. Another class of picture are the horizontal scrolls, often twenty yards in length, of ' which there are several In the collection. The exhibition , includes examples of all the princiLlal Japanese schools of painting—the Buddhist, the Japan, the Chinese, hum- orous caricatures, the popula4 and the naturalistic schools. The specimen of bamboo work include a great variety 'of articles. Some notion may be formed of the extensive use of bamboo in Japan when we say that in the cata- logue the articles are described under the followin4^ 'heads—Food, fences, carriages, weapons, tool,;; aaa implements, fishing, agriculture, domestic TAN wok/no tea drinking, toilet and personal oldeets. utensils, writing materials, and must-- We are told that "the instrument.:, smokin. propercie,s possessed by this giant lhave been well considered by the Janese. Its natural hollow formation eminently fits it, when cut into sections, to serYe as bottles, bowls, boxes, or tubes ; and the ingenious way in which the Japanese have contrived to turn this property to account is abundantly veritied by many articles in this collection. Its capacity for being readily split into long flexible, splinterless lengths,having great toughness and durability, has been most thoroughly taken advantage of by the Japanese in the varieties of plaited basket-ware made by them, from the rough tray of itinerant fish salesmen to lot, delicate covering of the porcelain saki-cup. There is, prebblily, no finer basket-work made in the world than the bamboo wok of Japan; and English basket-makers might study with bet some of the ancient examples of Japanese work exhibit, ed in the South Kensington Museum, and experiment as to the extent to which the material of which they are made might be profit- ably employed in this country. Other qualities of the bamboo have been taken advantage of in Japan. Its strength and lightness have fitted it for the construction of litters and other objects ; its toughness for the ropes which bind their tube, &c., its elasticity and regularity for their bows and arrows ; and its flint-like sharp edges for certain agricultural in- struments." In the collection there are many articles illustrative of interesting Japanese forms and ceremonies. The" Tea ceremony," the custom of present giving, the art of flower arrangement, and many domestic con- trivanceT and personal requirements are represented.

div.head: FATAL FALL FROM A BICYCLE.
div.p: A FATAL FALL FROM A BICYCLE.

On a Sunday evening in June, Joseph Hastings, aged 19 years of age, a pawnbroker's assistant, whose residence was 4, Fairclough's-yard, met with an accident whilst bicycling. He was riding an ordinary bicycle down one of the hills near Lymm when he lost control of the machine, which there- upon ran into the hedge pitching the rider over the hedge into a brook. The injured man was removed to the Warrington Infirmary, where he was found to be suffering from severe injuries to the spine. There he remained until Fri- day last, when, at his own request, he was allowed to go home to spend Christmas, but the poor fellow died on Monday night—Yesterday (Friday) an in- quest was held by the Coroner (Mr. H. C. Yates), at the Norton Arms, Bridge-st., Mr. E. Johnson being foreman of the jury.—Charles Hastings, of 4, Fair- dough's-yard, St. James's-st., the deceased's father, deposed that on Sunday June 22nd, the deceased left home well and hearty for Lymm on a bicycle. At half-past five that night witness beard that the deceased had had an accident and been taken to the. Infirmary. Witness had seen him off and on for six months. He died last Monday night at home hav- ing been removed from the Infirmary on the Friday. He blamed nobody for the accident. He bad only I learnt bicycling for three weeks but had had no pre- vious accident.—Ernest Bowden, surgeon' deposed that the deceased bad died from a fractured spine. It was by witness's permission that the deceased was removed home, as nothing more could be done for him at the Infirmary. De- ceased:bad told him he was hurled down an in- cline near Massey Brook in crossing the bridge and thrown over the parapet. The accident was fatal from the first. —Thomas Connor deposed that he waa uicycling with the ,deceased when the accident took place. They were riding alongside each other. They had ridden to Penketh together that morning, and the deceased had gone on all right during the day. Just before the accident happened, witness, who was riding alongside the deceased and crossing the bridge over Massey 'Brook, desired him to follow. The deceased made ilno answer, took his feet off the treadles, and lost contiol of the machine, which was thrown against the wall of the bridge,aud he fell. Stephen Craigen who also accompanied the deceased, corroborated, and stated that the rider and the machine were thrown over the wall together. The incline was not safe to ride a bicyle down. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death.
The Amphitheatre, the principal music hall in Ports- mouth, was burned to the ground on Thursday morning. A performance had been given In the building on Christ- mas Eve.

Advices received in New York from Peru state that a revolutionary attempt was made on the 2nd inst. out- side Lima by supporters of General Pierola. The attempt was frustrated but only after sharp fighting between the insurgents and the Government forces, in which forty lives were lost.

The Archbishop of Yorlr (the Right Rev. William Thomson, D.D.), died at Bishopthorpe Palace, York, on Thursday, at the age of seventy-one. His grace was seriously ill some months ages and although recovering for a time, was not strong enough to preside at the Church Congress at Hull, az he was announced to do. He remained in a feeble state and a few days ago had a serious relapse. His Grace was formerly Bishop of Gloucester and Bristol. A pay train has been vrrecked at Woodville,Mississippi, by an armed robber, who WAS subsequently captured. It has been decided by the Veterinary Society of Paris to apply Dr. Koch's remedy to animals suffering from tuberculosis. The remains of the late Sir Edgar Boehm were interred in St. Paul's Cathedral, on Saturday, in the presence et I a large and representative assemblage.

div.head: MA PARTY AND BALL.
div.p: MA PARTY AND BALL.

Last evening a tea party and ball for the members of the Conservative Club, was held in the club room. Tea which was commenced at six o'clock was pre- pared by Mrs. P. Pownall, about 60 persons doing justice to the repast. Dancing was commenced at seven o'clock and kept up till 10.45 p.m. Ac- companist, Mr. Finch of Warrington. The proceed- ings were superintended by Mr. P. Pownall.
EX.MOSION IN A SCHOOLROOM AT GREAT SANKEY.

An explosion, owing to the frost, occurred on Sat- urday morning in the Church schoolroom, Great Sankey. It appears that between ten and eleven o'clock, shortly after the fire had been lighted in connection with the heating apparatus, one of the pipes burst, cracking the wall and damaging the roof. It is fortunate that no children were in the room at the time, or a serious loss of life might have resulted. The damage is estimated at about .£2O. As a result of the explosion the usual Sunday school services were held in toe Board Schools.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF VICAR TO ST. PAUL'S, WARRINOTCIN.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF VICAR TO ST. PAUL'S, WARRINOTCIN.
r

The trustees of tha living of St. Paul's have unani- mously elected the Rev. Harry Vernon Pigott.M.A., late scholar of Oriel College, Oxford, as the Rev, S. Wilkinson's successor. The rev.gentleman is about 35 years of age, and is married. He has held cura- cies at Bolton-le-Sands and at Christ Church,Crewe. He has been highly recommended to the trustees by his rectors, the Rev. Alfred Birley and the Rev. G. J. Howson, and others, and it is hoped that a long career of usefulness in Warrington is before him. Mr. Pigott took the service on Sunday evening at St. Paul's Church, and we understand the appoint- m3nt is likely to meet with the full approbation of the congregation.

div.head: INSTITUTION OF THE REV. S. WILKINSON.
div.p: INSTITUTION OF THE REV. S. WILKINSON.

' A special service was held on Monday afternoon ,at Christ Church, Timperley, when the Rev. S. Wilkinson was formally instituted to the vicarage by the Lord Bishop of Chester. There was a fair congregation. The Bishop said their new pastor came to them as one who had laboured in the old diocese of Chester. He came to them with a good report, and he was one whom they might welcome as a true shepherd of the flock. And he was there that day publicly, and with the assistance of their prayers to institute him to his new post; and he believed that in instituting him to the spiritual care of the parish, he should be appointing a square man in a square place, or, if they would, a round man in a round place, one who would work har— moniously with his parishioners, and who would have the gift of calling out increasingly their har- monious co-operation with him. The usual deed of institution was subsequently read, the service con- cluding with the Benediction.

div.head: MORE IMPROVEMENTS FOR BRIDGE-ST,
div.p: MORE IMPROVEMENTS FOR BRIDGE-ST,
WARRINGTON.

Last week Mr. Thomas Sutton conducted a sale by public auction of two lots of property at Bridge-foot, Jot 2 consisting of a freehold dwelling-honse, with cottage adjoining, in the occupation of Mrs. Chrimes and Mrs. Byres; and lot 3, a freehold three-storey shop and furniture warehouse, in the occupation of Mr. R. W. Marsh. None of the lots at that time changed hands the reserve prices in no case being reached. Since the sale,however,we understand that the lots have been purchased by the Corporation for the sum of .£4,500. The object of the purchase is to enable the Corporation to effect further improve- ments in the widening of the street. The solicitors for the vendors are Messrs. W. D. Jeans, and Co., Warrington, and Messrs. Jeans and Morgan, Man- chester. It may be added that at the same sale other two lots of property were offered, one consisting of the old-established freehold brewery, known as "Mersey Brewery," with the outbuildings. stables, &c., adjoining, for many years carried on by Mr. Joseph Chrimes ; and the other lot compris- ing a freehold, fully-licensed public-house. the " Head,";Overton, Prod sham, and the dwell- ing-house and shop adjoining. £l,BOO was the highest bid for the shop at Bridge-foot and .£1,400 for the " Bull's Head." No offer was made for the brewery or dwelling-house, aithouzh there' was an offer of £2,000 for the brewery and public-house together. With regard to the proposed Bridge-st., improve- ment this will necessitate the pulling down cf the shop bought by the Corporation, but at present the shop is held by Mr. Marsh under a lease which does not expire till the 2nd of July. 1893. Tbis intended farther extension of the widening of Bridge-st ,wilt be all the more important in view of the fact that the corporation are, we believe, likely to s-on make- a move in order to bring about a wideniir.; of War- rington Bridge. which is now generally admitted to be much too narrow for the rapidly increasing traffic that has to pass over it.
