div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

WIFE DESERTION. Edward Burke was charged on Friday with leaving his wife chargeable to the Union. Mr. Shearer, relieving I officer, stated that the prisoner had been apprehended at Patricroft, on a similar charge in June last, and, for the present offence, in a public-house at Warrington. He had been convicted in the previous case but had never paid a penny. The prisoner admitted this, but said he ceuld not manage his wife on account of her drinking and carrying on. She went out of her mind with drink, and the house was broken up. He was sent to prison for a month's hard labour. NEARLY FROZEN TO DEATH. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, Frederick Bate, a puddler, living in Hoyle-st., was charged with having been drunk in Priestley-St. at a quarter to one o'clock on Sunday morning. P.C. Turner on his round found Bates lying on the ground" stiff as a block of wood" with the frost. The officer at first thought he was dead, but, after rolling him over,noticed that he breathed. He then got the assistance of P.C. Cooper, ! and they took the man to the Police Station, where he had to lie an hour and a half before the fire before he was fit to be placed in the cells.—The Mayor : You got him thawed, I suppose ?—P.C. Turner: Yes, sir.—The Mayor said Bates ought to be thankful for the care that had been taken of him ; otherwise he might not have been here for Christmas.—A fine of ss. was imposed. AN IRRECONCILABLE COUPLE. William Mather, a young man, was, on Tuesday, at the Warrington Borough Court, charged with having assaulted his wife, Mary Ann Mather, on the 19th Dec. Defendant pleaded guilty to having committed the offence " under great provocation." From the state- ment of Mrs. Mather it appeared that there had been some differences between her and her husband, and the latter had struck her and knocked her down. The pre- siding magistrate (Mr. R. Garnett) strongly advised the two to settle their differences and go and live happily with each other again, but there seemed on both sides an invincible determination not to do this. The defendant quite admitted that there was a time when he thought Mrs. Mather was the nicest young woman in Warrington, and on the other hand the complainant owned that at one time she thought a good deal of the defendant. But all that was changed now, and the wife said that all she wanted was an allowance for herself and two children, while the husband said he was quite willing to make this allowance. Under the circumstances, the magistrates bound the defendant over in £5 to keep the peace for six months.
THE CASE ON JOHN WAUREVOTON.

The notorious John Warrington, 17,was brought up on remand, on Friday,charged with stealing certain articles, the property of Louisa Dunbobbin, as reported above. The case having been proved, the prisoner, who pleaded guilty, requested that the magistrates would send him to the Workhouse or provide him with work. The Bench pointed out to him that they could not do the former, and that it was not their duty to find him work, they also reminded him that he had been in the Workhouse before and misbehaved himself. The Prisoner : I stopped until the weather was fine.—The Chief Con- stable : It is warm there.—Alderman Harrison : lam afraid, Mr. Hunt, there is a good deal of method in his madness.—The Bench sent him to prison for a month's hard labour, Alderman Harrison expressing a hope that the prisoner would come out a better lad in future. On Mr. Hunt asklng the prisoner whether he would pro- stiki.se to be better after coming out, he replied that he immediately burst out into a torrent of foul invectives a;ainst the Bench, and continued his impre- cations as he was n6ing hurried to the cells. MARRIED WOMAN. SERIOUS ASSACLT 61:7 A on Monday. a At the Warrington Borough Co: young man named Cornelius Lennon wag c;....7..?d with -ttiVing assaulted Isabella 'Harding and CharleS Henry 'Barnes in Dallam-lane on Saturday night. The Chief Constable said that Mrs. Harding was confined to her house,the assault having brought on a premature confine- ment. From the evidence that waS then given it riptt,alea that Mrs. Harding is the wife of an elkdihe driver em- ployed at Dallam Forge. Rather hat fn Saturday night she was taking her husband's supper and while going alongDallam-lane, the prisoner rushed out of a gateway and seized her by the throat. He pressed his fingers into her windpipe so that she was unable to call for help. A pin that she fastened her shawl with, however, ran into his hand and made him release his grasp when she at once ran towards a window from which a light shone and shouted " murder." This shouting attracted the attention of Charles Henry Barnes who went to his door and saw the prisoner again seizing the woman. Lennon ran away on seeing Barnes but the latter gave chase and caught him, and his brother coming to his aid they identified the pnsoner, who was afterwards apprehended. A sentence of six months' hard labour was passed on the prisoner and the two Barnes's were complimented by the Mayor on their conduct, and they were each awarded half-a-crown for their loss of time. LAWLESS PROCEEDINGS IN A LODGING HousE. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, Bodelia Knockton, a young woman who is often dealt with by the magistrates, was charged with having been found on Sunday morning, shortly after midnight,in the cellar of Ann Farrell, lodging-house keeper, Cloth Hall Yard, with intent to commit a felony. P.S. Taylor said that on Sunday night he was sent for to Mrs. Farrell's house and on searching the cellar he found the prisoner hiding behind some timber. Mrs. Farrell said that the prisoner was often brought into her house by her son,and the Chief Constable added that there had been several cases of robbery from lodgers at Mrs. Farrell's house,and he believed they were largely due to the landlady's son, and the prisoner who acted in connivance with each other. Alderman Harrison asked if such a house should be registered, and the Chief Constable replied that the matter had been reported to the committee, but as Mrs. Farrell had kept a lodging-house for thirty years and was not herself to blame for the robberies they did not like to knock her off the list—Ellen Farrell, daughter of the landlady, said that on Saturday night she saw her brother knock a man down in the kitchen and rob him while Bodelia Knockton held the door. The Mayor con- sidered this was a disgraceful state of affairs. The witness, in answer to a question said both she and her mother were frightened of her brother who often threat- ened them.—Alderman Harrison (to Mrs. Farrell ): You should turn your son out of the house.—Mrs. Farrell : He would kill me. The Chief Constahle told Mrs. Farrell that she would have to be taken off the list of lodging- house keepers. The Bench sentenced Knockton to three months' hard tabour, and as she was being taken from the dock she threatened " to do for" Mrs. Farrell when she came out.

and W. Owen.

AN UNWORTHY SoNT—James Gieeson, was charged with having assaulted his sister, Mrs. Higgins, on the 20th December.—lt was stated that defendant had struck his mother and knocked her down under a table, and when his sister intervened he assaulted her. Prisoner was

committed to prison for fourteen days. BRUNICENEJESS.-Wm. Gresty was ordered to pay Is. for having been drunk in Greenall-st. on the previous evenirg. WEDNESDAY —Before Mr. John Fairclough. • _ • _ __. • . . .

CHARGE OF THEFT.—John Warrington, a you-th about 16 years of age, who has on previous occasions been charged at the Court with various offences, was brought up in custody on a charge of having stolen a purse con- taining lid, and nine pawntickets from the dwelling- house of Ellen Imnbobbin, wife of a ship canal labourer, residing at 7, Croasley-st. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said that on Tuesday morning the prisoner went to Mrs. Dunhobbin's house and asked to be allowed to warm himsel4 at the fire. She allowed him to do so, and he remained about a quarter of an hour. Mrs. Dunbob- bin had occasion to leave the house for a minute or two, and on her return found that the prisoner had left. She discovered that her purse, which she had placed on the mantelpiece, was missing. She went in search of the prisoner, and found him, and charged him with stealing the purse, but he denied having done so. She threatened , to give him into custody, when he tried to drop the purse into a grid. He was remanded until Friday. FRlDAT,—Before Aldermen Harrison and Holmes. DRUNKENNESS.—Wm. Stockdale, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Wednesday night. He was discharged on payment of 2s. lock up fee.—Michael Quinn, puddler. drunk in the Market Place the same night, discharged on payment of the lock up fee. DRUNK AND THEFT. --Thomas Kelly was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on Wed- nesday afternoon, and also with stealing a glass, a crusher, and a jug the property of Mrs. Earle, of the Fox Inn. P.C. Dean deposed to being called in to the Fox Inn to eject the defendant and to his refusing to go and bang disorderly. Mrs. Earle and Wm. Taylor, postman, corroborated and proved the theft cf the articles. The pisoner was fined 20s. and costs, in .default a month's hard labour.
Mr. John Brancker was on Tuesday appointed chair- man of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, in succes- tdon to Mr. Alfred Holt, who declined to offer himself for re-election.
During the fog on Wednesday seven persons fell into the Clyde at Glasgow. Four were drowned.

THEFT.—Patrick Hulse, Ship Canal labourer, was charged with stealing 10s. belonging to a fellow labourer, named Arthur Brown. On Saturday afternoon the men were drinking together in the George Inn, and Brown placed half-a-sovereign on the table to pay for two drinks. The prisoner took up the coin and walked out of the place. Brown followed him and asked him to return the money but he declined to do so. Information was given to the police and the prisoner when apprehended by P.C. Woodrow made several contradictory state- ments. He was ordered to pay a fine of 20s. or go to gaol for a month. He went to gaol.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

The wholesale postponement -0-fin;Cches on Saturday caused intense disappointment all over the country. This time it was not confined to Rugby game only, but many Association matches had to be abandoned. Of course the North v. South fixture was included among the "slaughter of the innocents," and we shall have to wait some time before we can get an estimate of the relative strength of the two divisions. The North would have turned out precisely the team that had been selected, and there was every reason to believe that success would have met their efforts. In electing to throw in his lot with the northerners Martin Scott followed the natural course, as the birth qualification ought to have the first call. It is to be hoped that when the engagement is brought off we may see the same fifteen enter the field.

Some of the Yorkshire clubs managed to fulfil their engagements on Saturday, the most interesting of which was that between Bradford and Wakefield Trinity. The two clubs have been long estranged owing to ill-feeling engendered by occurrences in the past, and it seems a pity that when the breach was apparently healed over there should be another rupture. It appears that late in the game a try was allowed to Dewhurst, one of the Bradford men, which was hotly disputed by Jones, the Wakefield captain. Captain Rushworth, a member of the Yorkshire County Committee, was acting as referee, and ordered Jones off the field. He refused to obey orders, and the game came to an abrupt termination,the crowd making a hostile demonstration. Bradford had scored two goals and a try to nothing, but as time had not quite expired Wakefield intendto claim the result as a draw. Jones stated after the match that the differ- ence was solely between himself and the referee, an expression which was concurred in by Hawcridge, the Bradford captain.

Huddersfield lost theTr fixture with Hunslet, by the narrowest margin—a goal to two tries, both the latter points being the work of Dyson. Dewsbury had just as close a victory over Brighouse Rangers, whilst Hali- fax could only dispose of Leak; Parish Church by two tries. By way of contrast to these keen contests may be mentiond the runaway game at Ulverston, where the home team made a sorry exanylq pf Dalton to the tune of fiVe goals and four trifA,

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

It is generally understood that Association League matches must be played, however hard the ground, ex- cept fog interferes and makes it impossible to follow the ball. Well, this was the state of affairs at Bolton on Saturday, where play was altogether ont of the question The Wolverhampton Wanderers arrived at Pikes Lane after being delayed something like a couple of hours en route, and found the field of play enshrouded in inky blackness. Mr. Clegg, the referee, decided that football was not possible, and anothir &to will wai nave to be fixed upon. his

_ -- ---Aston Villa were an hour behind time at Accrington, owing to the tremendous block in the railway traffic, and this fixturestands over. There was some play to appease the spectators, but, of course, it was of no ac- count. They were more fortunate at Turf Moor, where the ground was in fairly good order, and as Notts had spent the night at Manchester, they were on the scene punctually. There was some fine football, the visitors winning by a goal to none. This was protested against on the plea of off-side, but unavailingly. The victory was of great importance to Notts, as it carried them ta the top of the League for the first time. The posi- tion is somewhat misleading, however, as Notts have run through one more fixture than any of their competi- tors.

All good judges of the dribbling code are unanimous in pronouncing the Sunderland team as one of the very first in the kingdom. They do not figure very well in the League table, 'tis true, but they have had more than their share of ill-luck. That they are a very for- midable lot was demonstrated on Saturday when they exactly reversed the result of their first contest with Everton, and beat them by a good goal to nothing. It is generally admitted that the advantage of ground is represented by a goal, which would thus place the two clubs of Everton and Sunderland on an exact equality. Their F. A. Cup tie on the 17th of January should pro- duce one of the very best contests of the competition.

Preston North End had little difficulty in shaking off Derby County at Dee:dale. As was the case every- where, the ground was in a hard and rugged state,which greatly detracted from the quality of the play. The home side had all the best of the argument, and ran ont out victorious by six goals to none. A new Scotch for- ward is shortly expected at Preston, and he is much needed seeing that James Ross is still indisposed. The Rovers were successful against West Biomwich Albion, but by a goal only.

IST. VOLUNTEER BATTALION SOUTH LANCASHIRE REGIMENT.
PRIZE DISTRIBUTION. The annual distribution of prizes won in the com- petitions at Widnes Range in connection with the Ist Volunteer Battalion, Prince of Wales Volunteers,

South Lancashire regiment, came off at the Drill Hall, Warrington, on Monday evening. Lieutenant- Colonel Bolton presided, and was supported on the platform by the Mayor (Alderman Francomb) Captain: and Adjutant Adam, Captain Gooch, Captain Baynes, Captain J. D. Buckton,Lieutenants Smith, Edelsten, Appleton, Fairclough, and Chorley, and the Rev. F. W. Willis,rector of Warrington, and . . . . .
, chaplain of the battalion. The battalion Eamf was present, and played inspiriting airs in admirable

style. The CHAIRMAN in opening the proceedings expressed his regret at the inability of Colonel Greenall, the com- manding officer, to be present. He thanked the donors of the prizes for their generous gifts from year to year, and hoped that the commanding officer would be able to arrange for some better system of giving these prizes in future, and they might perhaps be able to give an array of cups or something of the kind later on. They must, all, the Chairman re- . . . . „

marked, feel pleased at the presence of the Mayor of Warrington, who had kindly consented to come there to give away their prizes. The Chairman then called on the Adjutant to say a few words. Captain and Adjutant Adam said he was very glad to be able to attend there that evening, and say with the utmost sincerely that there had been a very great im- provement in all respects in the corps during the past year. There had been an infinitely better attendance at drill during the spring months before camp, which of itself was a very satisfactory thing, and consequently here had been an enormous improvement in the shooting of the corps. In 1888 the first year they rendered muske- try returns the figure of merit in the corps was only 42 something points. In 1889 it was 103 odd points,and this year it had gone up to 126 odd points, which he thought was very satisfactory,and extremely creditable to all con- cerned. The Adjutant expressed himself highly satisfied with the conduct of the recruits who had joined this year, and said more were wanted, and he hoped they would be got. There was, he said, going shortly, he believed, to be a recreation room established for the members of the battalion, where they could have a few games, and news- papers, and periodicals to make the men a suitable lounge, where they might smoke their pipes, and all that sort of thing, and be comfortable. He was glad to con- gratulate the corps on the improvement in the way in which they showed their respect to her Majesty's com- missioned officers. Throughout the year the men had endeavoured to treat their officers in a proper and re- spectful manner, •and saluted them as they ought to do in passing, with courtesy and deference. The Chairman concluded, after wishing all present a happy Christmas and a very prosperous New Year, by calling upon the Mayor to give away the prizes. The MAYOR, who was received with applause, said he was very pleased indeed to be there that night to dis- tribute the prizes, and he was sure that every one in the Corps would be pleased to make himself efficient during the coming year and odo better than ever he had done in the past. He found that they had got about 500 members in the Corps. Now, a town like Warrington with 50,000 inhabitants ought to have a Volunteer Corps of at least 1,000 members. (Applause.) He had always had great respect for the Volunteers and for the regular army ; in fact, he should very much like to have had a red jacket on himself, but circumstances had never pointed exactly that way. He thought he could spot a Volunteer in the streets of Warrington almost at any time in whatever garb he dressed. A man could not receive the training ho got in that room, he could net come into contact with such a military gentleman as their Adjutant—(hear, hear)— and with sdCll splendid Volunteers as there were, in that Corp ittiOut going a great e.,efti fkom time COn- tact ; and they might depend upon it that Englishmen who were trained with strict military discipline, would make better citizens, better workmen, and be smarter in their physique ; in fact would be improved in every possible way; and he did hope that those who had got friends not in the Volunteers woi.W.—show wa,0.b...1.......vary and also their bounden duty, to join a corps which presented so many advantages for them. Volunteer regiments were first established to pro- tect hearths and homes, and although the Volunteers might not be called away to foreign service, still he was quite certain that if any foreign foe should dare to attack our shores, they would meet splendidly equipped regi- ments who would show that if they were not regular soldiers of the line, they still had the bravery and the courage of their forefathers, and would give a good account of themselves. (Applause.) His Worship then proceeded to distribute the prizes. While the distri- bution was taking place, The CHAIRMAN rose and said that as an old and favour- ite officer had to be away very soon, he (the Chairman) felt he should not be doing his duty if he did not ask that officer to address a few words, before he went, to his fel- low-members of the regiment. The Chairman then called upon Captain Ridgway. Captain litndway then addressed the corps. He said as he had told them in years gone by he had an interest in the new range they wished to make at Rixton in cen- nection with the Manchester regiments. During the last _ _ .
two years, he had told them thy were getting on as well as could be expected, but pointed out the difficulties to be encountered; and he regretted to say that to a cer- .

tam extent they were not much further with the range than they were this time last year, when he spoke on the subject. They had a splendid piece of ground at Rixton for which they were now paying rent, and all they had to do was to set to work to make it into a range satisfactory to the Government Inspector, but unfortunately there was one difficulty, and that was a very serious one. It would cost something like £12,000 to make a suitable range. There was another difficulty —the new rifle. A rifle was formerly sighted up to two miles. This had now been altered to 1900 yards. That was a tremendous alteration, and it would necessitate great carefulness, when the new range was established. The Government had been approached soma 4 months ago on the question of raising the money, and they stated they could not find the amount. Now it was not desired that the Government should give the money, and it was determined to pledge the capitation grant in the future to repay tee sum if Government would only lend the £12,000. But they were not in a position to agree to that, they said, as it would require a private Act of Parliament to admit of their doing so. That had placed the Manchester regiments in a very unfortunate position. They had approached their members of Parlia- , ment,and one of these,Sir William Houldsworth,received a deputation of volunteer officers to see what scheme could be brought forwatd. The deputation laid their proposal before him and he promised to bring the matter before Mr. Goschen ; and he (Captain Ridgway), expected that gentleman had now heard or was about to hear of it. It all depended upon the answer from Mr. Goschen whether the Manchester regiments went into camp in the spring or in the summer. In the course of fur- ther remarks, Captain Ridgway said ho was very glad to see from the returns that his company so far as shooting was concerned had the third place in the corps, its figure of merit being 133, the highest being 143 and the second 136. That was very satisfactory, but he should much have preferred that they should have been No. 1. He could only ask his men to do their very best in the future, and he hoped yet to see them first on the list. He had done his utmost to encourage his men in good shooting, and if they had carried out the scheme he had put before them, he would have been giving £25 In prizes instead of the small amount he now gave, but still he could go home and say they had certainly left a handsome Christmas box in his pocket. He intended this next year to still give some prizes. His men would have the satisfaction of knowing that they could then pull out of his pocket £2O to £25. (Much applause.) Captain Ridgway then distributed the prizes won by the men of his company. Hie MAYOR then, at Captain Gooch's request, pre- sented the prizes of Captain Gooch's Company. A vote of thanks was then accorded to the Mayor, on the proposition of the CReinalisav, seconded by Captain BAYNES, to which the Mayor rdponded. Bolton mentioned that he had received a letter from Captain Ridgway apologising for his inability to be present. Captain Adam proposed a vote of thanks to the donors of the prizes. It was, he said, most kind of the trades folk of Warring- ton to show such a lively interest in that Volunteer corps. Their interest seemed unabated, and he trusted they , would continue to help the corps in the same way. The 1 vote of thanks was then accorded with acclamation. After the distribution, Lieutenant EDELSTON said it was nice to think that, as Volunteers, they got some addition to their comforts at Christmas by their connec- tion with the corps in the shape of the handsome prizes which had just been distributed. He hoped all who had received prizes, when they enjoyed them would think that it was some advantage to them to belong to the corps. On the other hand, he must remind them that there were responsibilities resting upon them in accept- ing the prizes. The public of Warrington had come for- ward very liberally in response to the applications which had been made to them by the sergeants. The trades- men gave the prizes, but they did not do so for nothing. They expected in return to find that the corps could do something in on emergency, and it was the bounden duty of the Volunteers to snake themselves efficient. (Hear, hear.) The lieutenant concluded by a reference to the shooting clubs which had been started, and re- marked that once a week, at a small cost, the men could go to the Widnes range and have as much shooting during the summer evenings as they wished. On the motion of Pioneer-Sergeant WARBURTON, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Lieutenant. Colonel Bolton, Captain Adam, and Lieutenant Edelston for their services, and the proceedings terminated. We may mention that several members of tin.) Parish Church choir kindly sang hymns in the course of the dinner.

div.head: WIFE MURDER AT LEITH.
div.p: WIFE MURDER AT LEITH.

On Saturday evening, Wm. Hendry, labourer, living in Burns-st., quarrelled with his wife. They are stated to have been under the influence of drink. Hendry had been home from work for a week, having met with an accident, and when the insurance agent called on Satur- day evening to pay him compensation money Hendry appeared to be very excited. Mrs. Hendry was lying on the floor, her face being covered with blood. The son stated that he saw his father kick his mother several times and then jump on her. The post-mortem examin- ation, which was held on Sunday showed that five of the ribs on the left side of the deceased were broken, and that her lungs and liver were evidently injured, while her head was frightfully battered, most probably by kicks. Deceased was about thirty-four years of age,
The prisoner was brought before the Leith magistrates, on Monday, charged with the murdar of his wife, on Saturday night, by beating and kicking her in their house. He was committed for trial.

• • Sir,—May I through your courtesy draw attention to the Religious Disabilities Removal Bill, introduced into Parliament by Mr. Gladstone supported by Mr. John . Morley and others? Making every allowance for the professions of loyalty made by leading Roman Catholics in this country, is it not wise to recall the assertion made by Lord Denbigh that he and his co-religionists are "Catholics first and Englishmen afterwards," and is not this the key-note of the whole question? Mr. Gladstone, in the past, then expressed himself, " N,3 more cunning plot was ever devised against the freedom,the happiness, and the virtue of mankind than Romanist-h." His opinions are further strongly reiterated in his pamphlet " Vaticanism." The historian Macaulay adds his testi- mony thus; "Among the contrivances for deceiving and oppressing mankind, the Church of Rome occupies the highest place." We must remember that the passing of thisßill necessitates the repeal of the Acts of settlement ; England, the land of freedom has allowed the Roman Church to advance steadily to political power, till only one single Act of Parliament now stands between us and • a Popish reign. Is it unreasonable to hope that Mr. Gladstone, with his extreme Liberal opinions, may re- • consider his decision in bringing forward the Bill 2—l am, sir, yours &c., 'December, 19th.

div.head: WEATHER AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE WEATHER AT WARRINGTON.

• The intense frost of Saturday and Sunday was felt no less severely at Warrington than at other places, but fortunately there has not been in this locality,as in some neighbouring districts, any fatality through the cold. In other respects no end of inconvenience was experienced by householders and tradesmen. In all directions water pipes and gas meters were frozen up and in many other instances a good deal of perseverance and ingenuity had to be exercised , in order to secure supplies of water for domestic ••uses. During Saturday's fog several tradesmen were -deprived the gas, and for the purposes of illumina- tion they had to fall back upon lamps and even the • humble and rather ineffectual "clip" was not despised. On Saturday the football match between Warrington and Broughton was cancelled, and on -Sunday the attendance at the different places of worship was very adversely affected by the cold and fog. Since Tuesday, a thaw has been in progress, alternating with a sharp frost on Christmas Day. INCONVENIENCE AT EARLESTOWN. In common with all other places,Easlestown,New- ton and the district have been visited with more severe weather during the past week, and the earth ' has for miles been covered with a white shroud of snow to the depth of several inches. The frost has been intense, and together with the fog that pre- :Tailed on Saturday, Sunday, and Monday, has ren- dered matters anything but pleasant. On Saturday the railway traffic became thoroughly disorganised, and the officials were unable to state with any . exactitude where the trains were from, or where they were going. Many were nearly two hours late, and others never arrived at all, and one or two • instances those who did get on the road failed, owing to some parts of the engine being frozen up. On Mondaynight many residences in the town were without gas and water, and much inconvenience was suffered thereby. Baths were trozen up, and the usual result of water pipes,cylinders. &c., burst- ing have followed. At the time of writing a wel- come thaw was in progress, and has every appear- ance of continuing. ExPLOSION IN A CHAPEL AT EARLESTOWN. On Sunday morning an explosion of an alarming ..and destructive character took place in the Welsh Chapel, in Houghton-street, Earlestown, caused, - there is no doubt, by the extremely severe weather. Mr. John Davies. the chapel keeper, went to the ,•-chapel, on Sunday morning before service, as usual, for the purpose of lighting the heating apparatus fire, in order to get the building warm for the con- gregation. He ignited the fire, and after seeing • that it was burning all right he went home to dress himself for service. After reaching home, he was alarmed by hearing a loud report; its of an explosion, • and going across to the chapel, found the portion , containing the heating apparatus, completely • wrecked. The shattered boiler he found about seven yards away from the chapel, and the roof of the room had fallen in, the walls also being down and the apparatus destroyed. Mr. Davies states • that had he followed his usual custom and remained in the building, he would have been standing Sop- , posite the boiler, and would most certainly have been. killed. He therefore considers his escape a :providential one. It is supposed that the water in the pipes had become frozen, and the boiler being • empty, it had on the inrush of cold water, exploded. The disaster will entail a heavy loss upon the wor- shippers, who are not very numerous.

div.head: • FROZEN TO DEATH AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: • FROZEN TO DEATH AT ST. HELENS.

From Friday night until Sunday forenoon last 'St. Helens was enveloped in one of the densest fogs .ever experienced in the district. The snow, which fell on Friday to the depth of several inches, still remained, and was accompanied by a bitterly cold wind. All outdoor occupations were at a complete standstill, and pedestrians had the greatest difficulty in making their way along the thoroughfares. Saturday was market day, but very few people attended, and the tradespeople generally state that less business was trans- acted on that day than on any occasion during the last few years. The steam trams only ran in the principal streets, and these were run at considerable inconvenience. The traffic on the railway was extremely irregular, many of the trains from the north and Warrington, Crewe, and London being two, and in some cases three, hours late. The sun shone for a brief period on Sunday at noon, and the fog gradually cleared. It again settled over the town on Sunday night, but cleared away on Monday morn log.

div.head: MAN FOUND DEAD IN THE SNOW.
div.p: A MAN FOUND DEAD IN THE SNOW.

About one o'clock on Sunday afternoon, the body of Jeremiah Tickle, a flint-glass worker, residing at Boundary-road, was found dead in the snow in some fields behind Cowley's Middle-class Schools, Cowley-hill, St. Helens. A number of lads were skating on a small pond behind the sehools. when one of them noticed a body lying about 1.5 yarls from the frozen water. They at once informed the pollee autlwities, and the body was subsequently identified as that of Tickle. It appears tha t the deceased leld he n missing since Friday night, . . .

and it is supposed that, while under the influence of drink, he stepped film a footpath near the fields and lost his way in the fog and snow. On Sunday afternoon the police authorities received information of two other persons bring missed from their homes, and they are making inquiries into the disappearances. On Tuesday forenoon Mr. S. Brighouse, •coroner, for South-west Lan- cashire, held an inquest at the Town flail, on the body of the deceased.lizabeth Ann Tickle, widow, said the _ . _

deceased was a flint-glass blower, and had wcrked at Messrs. Bishop's works. He loft home about halt-past eleven on Priday forenoon to go to his work, and she expected him hnme about half-past six or seven o'clock at night with .his week's wages. she never saw Lim alive again. He occasionally took drink but not to excess.—Flenry Hielicock, of E 3, Lawrenson-st., said he worked with tbo &ceased. They left the works together about half-past four on Friday, and called at the Lorne Hotel, where they stayed until about half-past nine. The deceased had different sorts of drink, includirig. bitter beer and whisky. There was a company of work- men together. fie fEd not know how much drink the deceased had, but he (witness) had a "tidy drop."—The Coroner : That is very expressivi..—Witness, in reply to other questions, said the deceased had as much drink as be (witness) had. Witness was about three-parts drunk. They were both capable of guir4:* home right enough. He left deceased at the corner of Nirkland-st. and West- field-st., and he understcod that the deceased was on his way home. The deceased at the end of Kirkland-st. should have turned to the left, but must have turned to ' • be
the right. It_was a very foggy night. It would

about—eleven o'clock at oig.ht sign ui4iness and deceased parted —Charles Sinrock, a bey, residing at 53, Stan- hope-st., deposed that he anti sotneotl ler boys were going across a field behind Cowley Schools to skate on a small pncl o Sunday *ftemova, when they found vest.

They traced footsteps from the vest to the spot where the betty of deceased was lying, about 100 yards away. I On Saturday witness found a jacket in the same field.— police-sergeant Sisson gave evidence that he proceeded to the field on hearing of the discoveries. The coat,vest,and hat were found in different parts of the field, which was an open one. Deceased was lying on his back, with one hand on his hip and the other on his chest. The foot- prints showed that deceased had walked three or four times round the field, that he had lain on his leack in one place, where there were marks that he had struggled, and he then seemed to have walked about a dozen yards further, where his body was f(4und. He found the sum of El. 13s. 7d. in his pockets. There were no marks of a struggle between two persons. Dr. Dale, assistant to Dr. M4Nicoll, deposed that he had made a post-mortem examination. There were no marks of violence. Exter- nally the nose, chin, ears, lips, and fingers were all severely frostbitten, and internally all the organs were perfectly healthy. He thought death resulted from ex- posure to the cold. Nearly all the blood and other fluid in the body was frozen, and pieces of ice were found in the stomach and in the heart. Every muscle of the body was very much contracted, showing that deceased must have had a frightful struggle when being overpowered by the cold. Towards the end the deceased would be- come delirious, and might think lie was getting into a comfortable bed —A verdict of Death from exposure to cold" was returned by the jury. EXTRAORDINARY DELAY OF AN INQUEST.

An inquest on the body of Ann Jane Buckley, eight years of age, daughter of Thomas Buckley, baker, 22, Napier-st., who died from burns received on the previous Tuesday, was arranged to be held at the St. Helens Town Hall, at 2.50, on Saturday afternoon. The jury, wit- nesses, and the police officials attended, but the coroner (Mr. S. Brighouse) failed to nut in an appearance. Many of the summoned jurors were tradespeople, and as the minutes rolled by there were complaints about their detention. At four o'clock a proposal was made that they should return to their homes and places of business, but it was decided to wait a little longer. At 4.20 a tele- gram was received from Mr. Brighouse, at Ashton-in- Makerfield, which stated that all appointments were dis- organised through the fog, but he hoped to arrive at half-past four. The jury accordingly stayed until the hour, and afterwards patiently awaited the arrival of five o'clock. A discussion then took place as to the rights of the jurymen on the non-arrival of a coroner, and as considerable doubt prevailed the chief constable was sent for. Mr. Wood attended, and it was pointed out to him by the jurors that they were suffering con- siderable inconvenience in their business engagements by their undue detention.—Mr. Wood said he was ex- tremely sorry that they had been kept there. If they refused to stay any longer—and he would entirely leave it in their hands—he could only tell the coroner that they had been present over two hours, and that they could not stay any longer. A jury said they were anxious to do their duty, and he thought they had waited long enough.— After some further conversation it was decided to wait another half-hour. But at 5.20, after the jury and wit- nesses had been detained two and a half hours, another telegram was received from the coroner intimating that he could not get a train from Byrn Station' and that he could not attend St. Helens that night. He asked for the jury to be discharged, and he would write further.— The Foreman then asked the Chief Constable to kindly excuse their service at the adjourned inquest.—The Chief Constable said he considered their request a very reasonable one, and promised to summon another jury. on Sunday it was stated that that the inquest would be held on Tuesday. On Tuesday forenoon, Mr. S. Brig- house, coroner, attended at the Town Hall, for the pur- pose of holding the inquiry. Addressing the new jury which had been summoned,he said they would no doubt be aware that a former jury had been summoned to take the inquiry on Saturday, but unfortunately he caused that jury a gocd deal of inconvenience and trouble by not coming to St. Helens. Those who knew the state of the weather on Saturday would know that it was out of his help, and since 1884 he never experienced a day like it. He was delayed all over the county, and when he got to Bryn Station, intending to come to St. Helens, no one knew anything about the trains, and as a matter of fact it took him three hours to get to Ormskirk from Bryn. If a delay like that should unfortunately occur again, instead of the jury being kept waiting when they lived in St. Helens or near to it. it would be best to send them away and tell them they could be sent for again if necessity arose. In fact, in order to form a precedent for the future, he wished it to be under— stood that if he was a guarter of an hour late, and if the jury did not. c,-1 msposed to wait, they could be die- and he (the coroner) would take the consequences. He regretted very much that the jury were kept last Saturday, and that there was a necessity for another jury to take the duties.—Evidence was then given to the effect that on the previous Tuesday morning the girl Buckley was downstairs in her nightdress, which caught fire. She was badly burned about the body, and died on Friday.— A verdict of" Accidental death,' was returned.

THE SHIP CANAL.

As previously stated, all the water has been pumped out of the locks at Latchford, and the men who have been at work ha.vebeen engaged in removing the vast amount of timber and other debris that was brought down by the last flood. There was a great accumulation at this por- tion of the works on account of the cutting narrowing for the tunnel which went under the railway line. The men have been engaged in removing the timber, but there are still many tons in the cutting. Although the water has been got away, nothing has yet been seen of the workman who is known to have been drowned, and it is now supposed that he must have been carried into the tunnel and overpowered by the debris. In that case, as a portion of the tunnel was filled up in order to save the railway, which was partially undermined, there is some doubt as to the body being found. There is still a considerable quantity of water in the canal cutting at the other side of the darn which was carried across the , canal at Morrisbrook, but it is, of course, very much lower than it was when the cutting was first flooded. A start has been made with a view to laying the founda- tion of the high level bridge, which will be mrried across the canal between Grappenhall-lane and Wash-lane. Steps, too, are about to be taken towards placing the swing bridges, as it is requisite that these bridges and the railway deviation should be got to work for some time before the canal is completed.

div.head: MODE WHEEL ARBITRATION.
div.p: MODE WHEEL ARBITRATION.

The arbitration to assess the amount of compensation to be paid by the Manchester Ship Canal Company for taking possession of the mills and water rights of the Mode Wheel Mills Company, Limited, under the powers of their Act of Parliament, was resumed on Tuesday at the Grand Hotel, Aytoun-st. Mr. Daniel Watney sat as umpire, the arbitrators being—For the Mode Wheel Com- pany Mr. John Cross, and for the Canal Company Mr. A. M. Dunlop. Mr. Thomas Rigby, of Sutton Weaver (secretary to the Cheshire Chamoer of Agriculture), said the mill was not worth the money asked by its owners from the Canal Company.—He was followed by Mr. William Wilson, auctioneer and valuer, of Manchester, who estimated the value of the Mode Wheel Mills at £15,201.—Mr. Richard Bradford, surveyor, also of Manchester, put the value at £ll,7Bl.—Mr. J. S. Peterson, valuer, put down between £12,000 and £13,000 as a fair valuation of the property in question. This concluded the evidence; and brought the proceedings to a close. The arbitrators made no intimation as to when their decision might be expected.

div.head: MOB VENGEANCE AT A FOOTBALL MATCH.
div.p: MOB VENGEANCE AT A FOOTBALL MATCH.
. _ .A.borrb 3.4 x, nm at es Ot t,

A WILD SCENE. An extraordinary and exciting scene was wit- nessed on Thursday afternoon on the Blackburn Rovers football ground at Ewood. The Rovers were advertised to play the Darwen men, and as there has always been a great deal of rivalry between the teams quite 5,000 spectators paid a double admis- sion fee, a large majority of them coming from Darwen. The sudden thaw of Christmas Eve was followed by a sharp frost, and when the time an- nounced for play arrived the field was literally a sheet of ice, on which it was impossible to walk with safety. Under these circumstances the committee of the Rovers, in view of the fact that they yesterday had to play Wolverhampton Wanderers,sent out their second team. The Darwen players followed on the field, but as soon as the spectators detected the composition of the Hovers' team there were angry shouts from the Darwen supporters, culminating in an uproarious command to their men to retire. After a consultation Marsden, the Darwen captain, led his men back to ' the dressing room amid tumultuous cheering. After a short pause the Darwen second string appeared on the field, but at this point a mob of spectators got over the barriers and overran the field, finally surrounding the dressing-rooms in a very threatening manner. It was announced that the match was abandoned and that spectators would receive tickets for another match. A large number availed themselves of this intimation and left tie ground, but some 2,000 remained, and after smashing the window of the dressing-loom, rushed to the goal posts, which they tore down and smashed to fragments. They then invaded the grand stand, and stripping the seats of the carpet coverings, carried them into the enclosure, and cut them to shreds. The huge flag which floated over the entrance gates was also torn down and destroyed. No such scene has been witnessed on the Blackburn Rovers' ground since the memorable occasion, nine years ago, when a dispute between Suter, of the Rovers, and Marshall, of Darwen, caused wild disorder.

Hill, and seconded by Mr. Ashley. ENTERTAINMENT AT CAIRO-ST. SCHOOLS.

The annual Christmas tea and entertainmenr in con- nection with Cairo-st., Unitarian Sunday school was held in the schools on Thursday evening. The Rev. F. K. Freeston, the pastor, presided. After tea a cantata entitled " Lampblack "was given by the children, the soloist being Miss Ida Allen, who took the part of " Lampblack," and Miss Rose Allen assuming that of " Nightingale." They were supported by a chorus of 20 voices. Kindergarten exercises were gone through, fol- lowed by an action song entited "The British flag." A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. H. Wright,who with Mrs. S. Wellings, and Mrs. Freeston, had trained the children. Games were indulged in until nine o'clock, after which the younger children were supplied with an orange each. The adults then commenced dancing to music contributed by Mr. Thos. Ford.

A WOMAN SEVERELY BURNED. On Tuesday a woman named Flannigan, wife of John Flannigan, of 25. Hopwood-st., Warrington, was admitted to the Infirmary, suffering severely from burns caused by her clothes getting alight as she was standing near the fireplace. C AITCH.L EY. Praatical Tailor. Bold-st.. Warrington.—Advt.

GREAT SANKEY Scitoor. BOARD. A meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday at the offices of the Clerk, Bewsey-st., there being present Captain Ridgwai in the chair, Mr. J. Wright, and Mr. J. Cook. The meeting was a Very short one, and the .business entirely formal. GREAT SANKEY BOARD SCHOOL CONCERT. Last evening week a concert in connection with the Great Sankey Board School was held in the schoolroom. Mr. J. C. Ridgway occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance. Under the con- ductorship of Mr. Clarke an excellent programme consisting of selections from the "Ancient Mari- ner," by T. Mee Pattison, was gone through by the scholars in a most praiseworthy manner. The second part of the programme consisted of glees, longs, &c., contributed by various friends, and was everything that could be desired. Accompanist, Mr. Parkinson of Warrington. During the interval prizes were given to the successful scholars in the recent examination. The proceeds are to be devoted to defraying the cost of prizes and a tea party for. the scholars. CRITCHLEY. High Class Tailor. Bold-st..Warrinaton.—Advt. DINNER TO FOOTBALL TEAMS. • '

On the invitation of Mr. William Tinsley,president of the Warrington Football Club, the members comprising the senior teams of the clubs were ' entertained to dinner at the Norton Arms Hotel, on Tuesday evening. Amongst the company present , were—Councillors Fleming and Pierpoint, Messrs. Thomas Morris, Percy Davies, John Evans, J. E. Warren (secretary). and Thomas Pemberton (treasurer.) Mr. and Mrs. Taylor catered in their usual well-known style, and it is needless to add that full justice was done to the many good things provided. Patriotic and suitable toasts were fre- quent, and mirth ruled supreme during the whole of the evening. Songs were given by Messrs. Davies, Warren, Evans, Holmes, and Daniels, and a humorous sketch of the company present by Mr. Percy Davies was heartily applauded. "Auld Lang Syne" brought en en-lovable evening to a close. "CETCIILEY, Practical Tailor, Bold-,t.,Wayriugton.—Adv

div.head: FOOTBALL MATCH YESTERDAY.
div.p: FOOTBALL MATCH YESTERDAY.

Yesterday afternoon there was a football match on the Wilderspool ground between the first teams of the War- rington and Rochdale St. Clements' Clubs. When it is mentioned that the score was one goal, five tries and four minors for Warrington and only two minors for St. Clements it will be seen that the game was rather one- sided, though it was perhaps not quite so one-sided as the score seems to indicate. The visitors at times played rather smartly, particularly when scrimmaging I and dribbling, but on the whole they were outplayed at all points of the game. Towards the end of the game, which was only a short one, Warrington had it practi- cally all their own way, and tries were scored rapidly. The scorers in the home team were Massey (2), Fair Turner (2), Holmas and Randalls. PARISH CHURCH YOUNG MEN'S ASSOCIATION. The annual soiree of this Association was held at the Conservative Club last night. Mr. J. Dillon's full band was in attendance, and the guests were numerous. Mr. G. Riley officiated as M.C. Dancing was commenced at eight o'clock and was continued for several hours.

THE LATE ARCHBISHOP OF YORK. The interment of the remains of the Archbishop of York has been fixed to take place on Tuesday in the churchyard at Bishopthorpe, near York.

div.head: IRISH LIBEL ACTIONS.
div.p: IRISH LIBEL ACTIONS.

A crop of libel actions will be the immediate result of the Parnell crisis in Ireland, arising out of the heated speeches made on both sides. Already several writs nay,; 111 hars of Porn. meat ilotre pro- minently amongst the litigants. _ COLLISION AT A LIVERPOOL STATION. A collision occurred yesterday forenoon between two North-western trains at Lime-st. Station, Liverpool, by , which several persons were severely shaken. A train from Wigan steamed into the station and along the platform when, 'from some cause, it ran with consider- able force into the rear of a train which had arrived from Leeds a short time before. The buffers of the engine, tender, and several carriages were broken. THE CONDEMNED CRIMINAL AT KIRKDALE. The execution of Macdonald for the Murder of Miss Holt, at Bolton, has been definitely fixed for Tuesday morning, the 30th inst., at her Majesty's prison, Kirk- dale, where the condemned man is under the constant care of the officials. The High Sheriff has decided to admit representatives of the Press into the gaol yard to witness the final scene. Berry will be the executioner. No attempt is being made by any of the prisoner's rela- tives to obtain a reprieve: FOOTBALL. WOLVERHAMPTON WANDERERS V. BLACKBURN ROVBRS. —Quite a holiday attendance assembled to 'witness this League match at Wolverhampton yesterday. The ground had been partly swept of a heavy fall of snow. The Rovers' defence was taxed to its utmost for twenty- five minutes, but the Wanderers, notwithstanding re- peated shots, failed to score. The Rovers then passed, and Rose had to stop several shaots. Wood scored for the Wanderers. Half-time score I—Wanderers 1 goal, Rovers nil. Final result :—Wanderers 3 goals, Rovers, nil. West Broom wich Albion beat Preston North End two to nil; Derby County and Bolton Wanderers one goal each; Everton beat Accrington 3to 2; Stoke beat Dar- wen 6 to 2; Aston Villa V. Sunderland: neither scored.

THE GREAT RAILWAY STRIKE. The strike on the Scottish railway continues, and it is calculated that between 8,500 and 9,000 men are now out. Many public works have had to stop owing to scarcity of fuel, and coal was sold in the streets of Glas- gow yesterday at famine prices. So far as Aberdeen is concerned the railway strike has collapsed. Nearly all the men have gone back to work. At a representative meeting of the citizens of Edin- burgh, yesterday afternoon, a committee was appointed to confer with the railway directors and servants as to a settlement of the strike. The committee embraces the Provosts of all the leading Scotch towns. The men at Dundee still continue firm, and the ranks of the strikers have been augmented. Yesterday a coil of telegraph wire was discovered on the rails of the Dundee and Abroath Railway. A public procession of railway men on strike at Carlisle yesterday, showed a great increase of strength. 1,200 RAILWAY MEN ON STRIKE AT HULL. Negotiations having failed, about twelve hundred men employed by the North-Eastern Railway Company, the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire Railway Com- pany, and the Hull and Barnsley Railway Company, at Hull,:have struck work, with a view of securing redress ot their grievances.
MR. O'BRIEN IN PARIS. PARIS.-Mr. O'Brien stated to an interviewer on Friday morning that the situation was so terribly serious that he could not yet make up his mind what to do.
WARRINGTON.
COMING EVENTS. On New Year's I)a3 the annual treat to the old folk of Warrington will be given in the Drill

To-morrow (Sunday) the Rev. F. K. Freeston will preach in Cairo-st. chapel. Subjects :—Morning, "Fax Vobiscum ;" evenings, "Old Year Musings." EMMANUEL CHURCH SALE OF WORK. We understand that the sum of £4O has been rea- lized by the two days' sale of work recently held in connectiou with Emmanuel Church.

A WARRINGTON DEACON. At the Advent ordination held by the Lord Bishop of the diocese at the Cathedral Church of St. Peter, at Liverpool, on Sunday, Mr. Harold Buckton, of St. Aidan's Theological College, Birkenhead, and Univer- sity College, Durham, was licensed as deacon to St. Peter's, Warrington.

TICE ANGEL'S SONG. In Cairo-st. Chapel, on Sunday, the Rev. F. K. Freeston took as the subject of his discourse, "The Angel's Song." A Christmas choral service was held in the evening, when special hymns and the anthems " Behold I bring glad tidings," and "Adeste Fideles," were sung by the choir.

SPECIAL SERMONS AT WYCLIFFE. On Sunday morning at Wycliffe Church, the Rev. J. Yonge preached a special sermon from the subject " Peace—the Result of Messiah's Reign.- In the evening he made special allusion to the late Miss J. Sanson, who was for many years .a member of the church and a teacher in the Sunday School. lIDLY TRINITY LITERARY AND DEBATING SOCIETY.

Last evening week an enjoyable soirée was held under the auspices of this society, dancing being kept up till the aarly hours of Saturday morning. The wnole of the arrangements were carried out by the committee, of which Mr. C. Spinks was the energetic secretary, and of which also the lady members were not:the least valuable and enthusias- tic part. Mr. T. Welsby and Mr. J. G. Johnstone kindly officiated as M.C.'s.

A SLIP AND A BROKEN LEG. As a Ship Canal labourer, named Charles Harvey, was walking over Warrington Bridge on Saturday night, about eight o'clock, on his way home, which is in Alice-street, he fell to the ground and broke his right leg. First aid was rendered by Police Sergeant Bowen (a member of the St. John Ambul- ance Association), who sent to the police station for bandages. The injured man was shortly after- wards removed on the police ambulance to the In- firmary, where he was attended by the senior house su geon, Dr. T. Smith.

THE PAROCHIAL SCHOOL, CHURCH-ST. 'The Rector has just received the following report (given in full) from the Department:—" The boys are in excellent order, and are taught with great care and success. Reading.is expressive and intel- ligent and handwriting generally bold and firm. Arithmetic is accurate and a very satisfactory num- ber of problems is worked, particularly in the third and fifth standards. The only weak points in the elementary work are the spoiling of all standards above the third, and the composition of the fifth and sixth. Both the class subjects are good, and the singing deserves praise." BILLIARD HANDICAP AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB. _ _

The distribution of prizes to the successful com- petitors in connection with the billiard handicap at the Conservative Club took place on Monday evening. The last game was concluded at eight o'clock, and entitled Mr. Daniel Rawling to GIP first prize. The other prize winners were—Thomas Acton, second ; H. J. Longton, third; fourth, William Booth; fifth, A. E. Peckham; sixth, J. E. Harrison; seventh, Frank Rutter; and eight to sixteenth, Messrs. Reginald Rigby, William Davies, Thomas Peak, lames Holland, Henry Johnson, Harry Jackson, Jacob bailey, JOlin -TosLßnh Strettle. Prior to the distribution of the prizes a number or members had supper together in the Assembly-room. Mr. R. Pierpoint presided, and presented the prizes, ' an enjoyable evening being spent. EMPIRE TIIEATRE OF VARIETIES. The programme of this place of entertainment during the week has been of a versatile and very attractive description, including some new and striking items; and preparations are being made for the coming delectation of the public which are com- mensurate with the character of the season. Fiske and Muldoon produce exuberant mirth by their per- formances, and the "Acrobatic Micks " forms another prominent feature of the entertainment. Prof. Devereaux with his wonderful troupe of per- forming dogs exemplifies to an amazing degree the extent to which dogs may be trained to achieve feats one would suppose immeasurably beyond the capacity of the canine race. One of his animals so far outdoes the record of such achievements as to perform the astounding exploit of catching a real ball fired from a real cannon. Mr. T. Raynor, char- acter comedian, Miss Kate Dalton, serio-comic and characteristic vocalist, Messrs. Murphy and McGuire, comedians, dancers, &c., Mr. Oscar Hamp- son, negro comedian known as "the imp of dark- ness," Miss Ada Whitton, male impersonator, and others, constitute the remainder of the talent. The entertainment concludes with a highly diverting farce " Razoriana." Two grand special perform- , anees were given on Christmas Day. CRITCHLEY'S Tailoring meets the times.—Advt.

:NG MURDER. BY A 2TEPHEIV.
Leatherdale

At Salcot, a village in Essex, Arthur aged 17, has been arrested for the murder of his uncle, Joseph Leatherdale, a farmer. The homestead in which the two lived is in a secluded part of the county. Mr. Leatherdale disappeared on Saturday, but it was not un- til Tuesday that suspicions were aroused as to his ab- sence. When the nephew was questioned with regard to his uncle's disappearance he changed colour, and said he had received a letter from him. The answer was considered unsatisfactory, and the youth was requested by the police to join in the search. The farmer was found dead in his own house. His body had been I thrust into a cupboard, and there was a deep gun-shot wound at the back of his neck, around which a halter had been tightly drawn. Some percussion caps that fitted one of the farmer's guns were found in young Leatherdale's pockets. Accused of the crime, he said that he had not murdered his uncle. He got someone else to do it, and told the man he could have all the money in his uncle's pocket as a reward for the deed. There were, he asserted, several accomplices, but he did not intend to reveal their names. The inquest has been opened and adjourned until next week. The prisoner. brought before the Colchester magistrates on Wednes- day, made a voluntary statement of his complicitY in the crime, but denied that he was the actual murderer.

THE MARMALADE TRADE,—The severe weather we have recently experienced in this quarter has extended as far south as Seville. It is in the neighbourhood of Seville, that the oranges best suited for marmalade mak- ing are grown. A recent frost (the like of which has not been experienced for ten years), has played havoc with the fruit, and, although the full extent of the dam- age is not yet known, it is believed that fully one half the orange crop has been destroyed. Luckily one ship- ment had been made to Liverpool before the disaster eccurred, by SS " Lurburan," which has just arrived. The Liverpool firm of W. H. Flett, Limited, have been fortunate enough to have a large consignment on Board this vessel, but they do not anticipate getting nearly sufficient to meet the demand for their well knovrn marmalade, the sale of which is ever increasing.

COUNTY OF CHESTER, TO WIT. INTOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENICR al. QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY F. CHESTER. will be holden at the Castle of Chester, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the sth day of January next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Ecidisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury tor the Chester District must be in attendance ;a the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the sth day of January next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. WHEREAS at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, holden at Nether Knutsford, in and for the County of Chester, on Monday, the 13th day of October, 1890, a Provisional Order was made in the words following, that is to say— At the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace of our Lady the Queen holden at Nether Knutsford, in and for the County of Chester, on Monday, the 13th day of October, 1890. • WHEREAS a proposal in writing, dated the 13th Septem- ber, 1890, bath been laid before this Court under the hands of the Honourable Cecil Thomas Parker, Benjamin Chaffers Roberts, Esquire, John Thompson, Esquire, James Sweten- ham, Esquire. and The Reverend Edward Augustus Pitcairn Campbell, five of Her Majesty's Justices of the Peace for the County of Chester, to vary the existing boundaries of the Highway District of the Western Division of the Hundred of Broxton by including within such District and adding thereto the Township of Huntington, in the said County ef Chester. NOW IT IS ORDERED by this Court, upon consideration of such proposal, that the said Township of Huntington shall, from and after the 25th day of March. 1891, be added to and form part of the said Highway District of the Western Division of the Hundred of Broxton, in the said County, for ' all the purposes of the Highway Acts. AND IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the said Township of Huntington shall be entitled to elect one Waywarden to form part ot the Highway Board for the said Highway District. AND IT IS ALSO FURTHER ORDERED that the said Township of Hunting- ton so included in such Highway District as aforesaid, shall not be liable to contribute to any Debts or Loans contracted by the said Highway Board for such Highway District prior to the said 25th day of March, 1891. AND THIS COURT doth hereby appoint the General Quarter Sessions of the Peaco to be held at CHESTER CASTLE, in and for the said County of Chester, on MONDAY, the sth day of January, 1891, for the purpose of taking into consideration the Confirmation of the Pro- visional Order hereby made. NOTICE IS HEREBY ALSO GI TEN, that the Confirma- tion of the said Provisional Order by a Final Order will be taken into consideration by the Justices at the Court of General Quarter Sessions to be held at CHESTER CASTLE aforesaid, on MONDAY, the sth day of January next. THE COURT will be Adjourned to the Court House, Nether Knutsford, on WEDNDSDAY, the 7th day of January next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. The hearing of all appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow,Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last mentioned Hundreds will takeplaCe at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the °petting of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the 9th day of January next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS. Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Cheater, 16th December, 1890.
